ESE 4007 Study Pack

Smart Grid Technology. One-shot notes, then every shortlisted past-paper topic (2020-2023) with full answers, slide figures and worked numericals. Your place, theme and text size are remembered on this device.

24-hour priority list

You answer 3 of 4 questions in each part, so each part has its own list. Study down both lists until the green pass line: about 4 h for Part A and 4 h for Part B, which leaves time for sleep and a last read of the one-shot notes. Alternate between parts (A block 1, B block 1, A block 2 …) so neither is left short. Chance: how often the topic came up, newer papers weigh more (2023 ×3, 2022 ×2, 2020 ×1). Covered: share of that part's past-paper marks you have studied once you finish the row.

Next if you have time: B4 (swing equation and equal area) is the one hard topic that keeps coming back; the power-angle graph makes it quick to understand. B5 (2020 numerical) appeared only once, in the oldest paper, so learn it last.

One-shot notes: ESE 4007 Smart Grid Technology

Smart grid in one line

Old grid + sensors (eyes) + two-way communication (nerves) + automatic control (brain). Digital, two-way power and data, distributed generation, self-healing, active customers.

Drivers: demand, ageing assets, reliability, renewables, climate, efficiency, customer choice, ICT. Bangladesh: losses/theft, peak gap, blackouts, renewables target, costly imported fuel.

Stakeholders

Generators, transmission/system operator (PGCB, NLDC), distribution utilities (DPDC, DESCO, BREB), consumers/prosumers, regulator (BERC, SREDA), vendors/ICT, aggregators, researchers/standards bodies.

Active vs passive distribution

Passive: no DG, one-way, fit and forget, simple protection. Active: DG/storage/flexible loads, two-way, real-time control.

Loop: measure → communicate → state estimate + forecast → control (Volt/VAR, DG dispatch, reconfiguration, DR, FLISR) → act.

Three technology families

ICT: fibre, PLC, ZigBee, Wi-Fi, WiMAX, cellular; protocols IEC 61850, DNP3. Sensing/control: smart meters, PMU, sensors, IEDs, SCADA/DMS, automation. Power electronics: inverters, FACTS, HVDC; storage: batteries, pumped hydro, flywheel, supercapacitor, SMES, CAES.

DG and microgrid

DG = small (kW-50 MW) generation in the distribution network near loads. Advantages: lower losses, better voltage, reliability, deferred investment, renewables, CHP, quick.

Microgrid: DGs + storage + loads + MGCC + static switch at PCC. On-grid: grid sets V, f; DGs in PQ mode. Islanded: switch opens, V/f or droop control, shed non-critical loads, resynchronise later.

Communication

SCADA: field devices/RTU/IED → network → master station + HMI. Advantages: real-time monitoring, remote control, faster restoration, efficiency, data, safety.

HAN (home, 10-100 m: ZigBee, Bluetooth, Wi-Fi) → NAN (neighbourhood, 1-10 km: RF mesh, PLC, WiMAX) → WAN (backbone: fibre, WiMAX, LTE).

Smart meter and AMI

Meter → NAN → concentrator → WAN → head-end → MDMS → billing, OMS, DMS, portal.

AMR one-way billing reads; AMI two-way: interval data, remote connect/disconnect, ToU and prepaid, outage alerts, HAN link.

DSM

Change timing/amount of use to flatten the load curve. Peak clipping (cut peak: direct load control), valley filling (add off-peak load: night EV charging), load shifting (move peak to off-peak: ToU, thermal storage). Plus conservation, load growth, flexible load.

PMU and WAMS

Measures V, I phasors + frequency + ROCOF, GPS time-stamped (1 μs), 25-60 per second. Blocks: CT/PT inputs, anti-aliasing filter, A/D, GPS + phase-locked oscillator, DFT microprocessor, modem.

WAMS: PMUs → local PDC → super PDC → monitoring, state estimation, protection.

Load flow

Buses: slack (V, δ), PV (P, |V|), PQ (P, Q). Methods: Gauss-Seidel (simple, slow), Newton-Raphson (fast convergence), fast decoupled (fastest), DC (linear).

Smart grid needs: stochastic, three-phase unbalanced, DG and two-way flow, high R/X robust, real-time with PMU/AMI data, large-scale.

Analysis tools

Contingency = what if one element trips (N-1). SSA = steady post-contingency limits check: secure / alert / emergency. SCOPF = cheapest dispatch still secure after contingencies. DSOPF = OPF + time + uncertainty (adaptive dynamic programming). Congestion = line at its limit: re-dispatch, FACTS, pricing. GIS: asset maps, outages, crews, planning.

Multi-agent systems

Agent: autonomous, reactive, pro-active, social. IDAPS agents: control (island/reconnect), DER, user (critical loads), database. Meter MAS: meter agents → collector agents → billing, database, monitoring agents.

Ybus

Yii = sum of admittances at bus i (including shunt); Yij = −yij. KCL at each bus ⇒ Ii = ΣYijVj ⇒ Ibus = YbusVbus. Symmetric, sparse.

Infinite bus: constant V and f whatever the power.

Frequency control

Frequency = generation-load balance. Governor chain: fly-ball → linkage → hydraulic amplifier → valve; droop R leaves Δf = −RΔPL/(1 + DR).

LFC loop: governor 1/(1 + sTg) → turbine 1/(1 + sTt) → 1/(2Hs + D), feedback 1/R. AGC: integral of ACE = ΔPtie + BΔf; restores 50 Hz and tie flows; essential with renewables.

Reactive power and voltage

P ↔ frequency, Q ↔ voltage. Q devices: AVR/excitation, shunt capacitors/reactors, series capacitors, synchronous condensers, OLTC, SVC, STATCOM, smart inverters.

AVR: sensor → compare with Vref → amplifier → exciter → field. SVC = TCR + TSC + filters. Pmax = EV/X: raise E, V; cut X.

Rotor-angle stability

Steady-state = small slow changes; transient = large sudden faults. Swing: (H/πf0)d2δ/dt2 = Pm − Pmaxsinδ.

Small disturbance: Ps = Pmaxcosδ0, s = ±j√(πf0Ps/H) ⇒ ωn = √(πf0Ps/H); Ps < 0 unstable.

EAC: stable if A2 (decelerating) can equal A1 (accelerating) before δmax = 180° − δ0. cosδcr = (π − 2δ0)sinδ0 − cosδ0.

Machine numerical (2020)

I = 0.625∠−36.87°. No saliency: E′ = 1 + j0.3I = 1.1226∠7.68°, P = 3.742 sinδ.

Saliency: EQ = 1 + j0.6I = 1.2612∠13.76°; Id = 0.4832; E′q = 1.1162; P = 3.721 sinδ − 0.833 sin2δ.

Voltage stability

Causes: heavy load, long lines, Q shortage/generator limits, outages, OLTC action, motor loads. Prevent: Q reserves, capacitors/SVC, generator V set-points, block OLTC, re-dispatch, load shedding, PMU monitoring.

Techniques: P-V, Q-V, CPF, modal analysis, indices (L-index, VIPI), dynamic simulation, PMU/AI. VIPI = angle between load vector and the midpoint of the two load-flow solutions → 0 at collapse.

Power quality

Sag, swell, interruption, transients, harmonics, flicker, unbalance, frequency deviation. Matters for sensitive loads, heating/losses, inverter-rich grid. PQ audit: measure, find source, fix, comply.

Intelligence tools

ANN: layers of weighted neurons trained on data; forecasting, security assessment, fault detection, theft detection. ES: knowledge base + inference engine; alarm processing, fault diagnosis, restoration.

AHP: hierarchy → pairwise 1-9 → weights (eigenvector) → CR < 0.1 → synthesis. Computational challenges: size, uncertainty, real-time, non-linear optimisation, multi-time-scale, data/cyber, models.

Cyber security

Interoperability = exchange and use information (IEC 61850, CIM, DNP3, IEEE 2030). Threats: malware, DoS, man-in-the-middle, meter tampering, FDI, GPS spoofing; huge attack surface.

FDI: a = Hc passes the residual test → wrong state, wrong dispatch, overloads. Mitigation: defence in depth, authentication, encryption, protected key meters, PMUs, anomaly detection, response plans, training.

Renewables, V2G, barriers

Renewable challenges: variable, uncertain, low inertia, distributed (forecasting, storage, protection, PQ, markets). V2G: bidirectional charger, charge off-peak, discharge at peak, frequency regulation; battery wear.

Barriers: cost, regulation, standards, security, skills, consumer acceptance → phased rollout, policy, standards, training, awareness.

Section A: Smart grid concepts, distribution, communication, metering, PMU, load flow and analysis tools

Past-paper questions · Must study

  • 2023 Q1(a) [10] Make a comparison between the conventional power system and a smart grid.
  • 2022 Q1(b) [10] Who are the main stakeholders of smart grid systems? Describe their functions.
  • 2022 Q1(c) [10] Mention the key drivers of smart grid. Is a smart grid necessary for Bangladesh? Justify your opinion.

★ REMEMBER IT
  • Smart grid = old grid + eyes (sensors, smart meters, PMUs) + nerves (two-way communication) + brain (automatic control, software). Old grid: one-way, central, blind, manual. Smart grid: two-way, distributed, observable, self-healing.
  • Stakeholders: generators, transmission and distribution utilities, consumers/prosumers, regulators, equipment vendors, ICT (information and communication technology) providers.
Before you start: what makes a grid "smart"

The old grid is like a one-way water pipe system: big power stations push electricity through transmission lines and distribution feeders to homes, and the utility learns about a fault only when customers phone in.

A smart grid adds a nervous system to that pipe system: sensors and smart meters everywhere (eyes), two-way digital communication (nerves), and computers that analyse and control automatically (brain). Now power and information both flow both ways, homes can also generate (rooftop solar), and the grid can heal itself.

Definition (2020 1a)

A smart grid is an electricity network that uses digital and other advanced technologies - two-way communication, sensing and measurement, automatic control and computer intelligence - to monitor and manage the transport of electricity from all generation sources to meet the varying demands of end users, so that the grid is more reliable, efficient, secure, economical and environment-friendly. (Momoh: "the integration of power, communication and information technologies for an improved electric power infrastructure serving loads while providing an ongoing evolution of end-use applications".)

Conventional power system vs smart grid (2023 1a)
FeatureConventional gridSmart grid
TechnologyElectromechanicalDigital
CommunicationOne-way (or none)Two-way, real time
Power flowOne-way: generation → consumerTwo-way: consumers can also supply (prosumers)
GenerationCentralised large plantsCentralised + distributed (DG, renewables, storage)
Sensors / monitoringFew sensors, manual monitoringSensors and PMUs throughout, self-monitoring
Fault handlingManual restoration; failures and blackouts spreadSelf-healing: automatic fault detection, isolation and restoration; adaptive protection, islanding
ControlLimited, centralPervasive, distributed and automatic
CustomerPassive, flat tariff, monthly manual readingActive participation: smart meters, time-of-use pricing, demand response
Equipment checkingManual, time-based maintenanceRemote monitoring, condition-based maintenance
Efficiency and environmentHigh losses, hard to integrate renewablesLower losses, easy integration of renewables and EVs
Architecture of smart grid design and functions of its components (2020 1b)

The smart grid architecture has three layers working together: (1) the power layer (generation, transmission, distribution, consumers); (2) the communication layer (WAN, NAN (neighbourhood area network), HAN (home area network) networks); (3) the control and application layer (control centres, data management, markets).

ComponentMain function
Smart generation (central + renewables + storage)Supplies power flexibly; renewables and storage dispatched with forecasts; generators respond to AGC (automatic generation control) signals
Smart transmission (PMU/WAMS, FACTS (flexible AC transmission systems), HVDC (high-voltage direct current), substation automation)Wide-area monitoring and control, higher transfer capacity, stability, fast fault clearing
Smart distribution (DMS, feeder automation, DG (distributed generation), microgrids)Self-healing feeders, Volt/VAR control, DG integration, outage management
Smart meters and AMI (advanced metering infrastructure)Two-way metering, time-of-use pricing, remote connect/disconnect, outage detection
Customer side (HAN, smart appliances, EVs, rooftop PV)Demand response, energy management, prosumer generation, V2G (vehicle-to-grid)
Communication networkCarries measurements and control signals securely in real time
Control centre / applications (EMS, SCADA (supervisory control and data acquisition), DMS (distribution management system), MDMS (meter data management system), analytics)State estimation, optimal power flow, security assessment, forecasting, billing
Energy storage and power electronicsBalance variable renewables, voltage and frequency support
Key drivers of the smart grid (2022 1c)
  • Growing and changing demand (more air-conditioning, EVs, digital loads) and need to reduce peak demand.
  • Ageing infrastructure that must be replaced anyway; better to replace it with smart equipment.
  • Reliability and power quality: costly blackouts (e.g. US-Canada 2003; Bangladesh 2014 and 2022 national blackouts), sensitive digital loads.
  • Integration of renewables and DG (solar, wind) that are variable and distributed.
  • Climate change and environmental targets: cut CO2 by efficiency and renewables.
  • Efficiency and loss reduction; better use of existing assets.
  • Customer empowerment and new markets: choice, demand response, prosumers, EVs.
  • Security (physical and cyber) and advances in ICT that make it affordable.
Is a smart grid necessary for Bangladesh? (2022 1c)

Yes. Reasons:

  1. High system losses and electricity theft in distribution; smart/prepaid meters and AMI cut non-technical losses (prepaid smart meters are already being installed by DESCO (Dhaka Electric Supply Company), DPDC (Dhaka Power Distribution Company), BREB (Bangladesh Rural Electrification Board), WZPDCL (West Zone Power Distribution Company Ltd)).
  2. Large gap between peak and off-peak demand (evening peak); DSM (demand side management) and time-of-use tariffs can flatten it and avoid costly peaking plants burning oil/diesel.
  3. Frequent load shedding and grid failures (national blackouts of 2014 and 2022); WAMS (wide area monitoring system), PMUs and automation improve stability and restoration.
  4. Government targets for renewables (solar home systems, rooftop net metering, solar parks, wind); a smart grid is needed to integrate variable renewables.
  5. Rapid growth of demand, industrial zones and EVs (easy-bikes) that need managed charging.
  6. Imported fuel (LNG, coal) is expensive; efficiency and peak reduction save foreign currency.
  7. Climate commitments and vulnerability; smart grid supports clean energy and resilience to cyclones/floods (microgrids for islands and remote areas).

Challenges are cost, skills, regulation and cyber security, so it should be built step by step (prepaid meters → AMI → SCADA/DMS → WAMS → microgrids).

Main stakeholders and their functions (2022 1b)
StakeholderFunction
Generation companies (public, IPPs, renewable developers)Produce power, provide flexibility and ancillary services (frequency, reserve)
Transmission operator (PGCB in Bangladesh) and system operator (NLDC)Operate the high-voltage network, balance supply and demand, ensure security and stability
Distribution utilities (DPDC, DESCO, BREB, NESCO (Northern Electricity Supply Company), WZPDCL)Deliver power to consumers, install smart meters, DMS, integrate DG, outage management
Consumers / prosumers (residential, commercial, industrial)Use energy, take part in demand response, generate with rooftop PV, own EVs and storage
Regulators and policy makers (BERC, Power Division, SREDA (Sustainable and Renewable Energy Development Authority))Set tariffs, standards, rules for cost recovery, renewables and data privacy
Equipment and technology vendors, ICT/telecom providersSupply meters, sensors, communication networks, software and cyber security
Energy service companies, aggregators, retailersOffer energy-efficiency, demand response and EV-charging services
Researchers, standards bodies (IEEE, IEC (International Electrotechnical Commission), NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology (USA)), universities)Develop technologies, standards for interoperability and security, train manpower

Memory trick: Smart grid = "Eyes (sensors), Nerves (communication), Brain (control)" added to the old grid. Comparison key words: digital, two-way, distributed, self-healing, active customer.

A3 Enabling technologies: information and communication; sensing, measurement, control and automation; power electronics and energy storage Very likely · 100%Easy

Past-paper questions · Must study

  • 2023 Q1(c) [15] Provide an overview of the following technologies required for smart grids: (i) information and communication technologies, (ii) sensing, measurement, control and automation technologies, (iii) power electronics and energy storage.
  • 2022 Q2(b) [12] Describe the roles of sensing, measurement, control and automation technologies for a smart grid.
  • 2020 Q1(c) [15] Provide an overview of the following technological requirements for a smart grid: (i) information and communication technologies, (ii) sensing, measurement, control and automation technologies, (iii) power electronics and energy storage systems.
★ REMEMBER IT
  • Enabling technologies, I-S-P: Information & communication (networks, protocols, cyber security), Sensing, measurement, control & automation (smart meters, PMUs, SCADA (supervisory control and data acquisition), IEDs), Power electronics & energy storage (inverters, FACTS (flexible AC transmission systems), HVDC (high-voltage direct current), batteries).
Before you start: the three technology families

To make the grid smart you need: (1) a way to talk (information and communication technology, ICT (information and communication technology)), (2) a way to see and act (sensors, meters, controllers, automation), and (3) a way to shape and store power (power electronics converts AC/DC and controls flows; storage keeps energy for later).

(i) Information and communication technologies (ICT)
  • Provide two-way, fast, reliable and secure exchange of data between all parts of the grid; the backbone of the smart grid.
  • Wired: optical fibre (high bandwidth, immune to interference; WAN (wide area network) backbone, substations), power line communication (PLC, uses the power cables; meters, distribution), DSL (digital subscriber line), Ethernet.
  • Wireless: ZigBee and Bluetooth (HAN), Wi-Fi/WLAN, RF (radio frequency) mesh (NAN), WiMAX (Worldwide Interoperability for Microwave Access (IEEE 802.16)), cellular 3G/4G/5G and LTE (NAN/WAN), satellite (remote sites).
  • Networks: HAN (home area network), NAN (neighbourhood area network)/FAN, WAN (A5); protocols and standards: IEC (International Electrotechnical Commission) 61850 (substations), DNP3 (Distributed Network Protocol 3), IEC 60870, Modbus, IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.15.4, ANSI (American National Standards Institute) C12, CIM (common information model).
  • Information technology: data management and cloud, big-data analytics, state estimation software, GIS (geographic information system), cyber security (encryption, authentication, firewalls), interoperability.
(ii) Sensing, measurement, control and automation technologies (2022 2b)
TechnologyRole in the smart grid
Smart meters / AMI (advanced metering infrastructure)Measure consumption at short intervals; enable time-of-use pricing, demand response, outage detection, remote connect/disconnect, power quality data
PMU (phasor measurement unit) / WAMS (wide area monitoring system)GPS-synchronised phasors 30-60 times/s; wide-area visibility, stability monitoring, faster state estimation (A8)
Sensors: line sensors, dynamic line rating, transformer and cable condition monitors, fault indicators, weather sensorsDetect faults, overloads, hot spots; allow higher line ratings and condition-based maintenance
IEDs (intelligent electronic devices, digital relays)Measure, protect and control locally; communicate with SCADA
SCADA, EMS (energy management system), DMS (distribution management system)Supervise and control the whole system remotely (A5)
Substation and distribution automationAutomatic switching, reclosers, sectionalisers, FLISR (fault location, isolation and service restoration) self-healing, Volt/VAR optimisation
Advanced control methodsAdaptive protection, wide-area control, AGC (automatic generation control), intelligent agents, optimisation and AI (B8)

Together they let the grid see itself in real time, decide quickly and act automatically, improving reliability, efficiency and DG (distributed generation) integration.

(iii) Power electronics and energy storage
  • Power electronics: converters/inverters that connect PV, wind, batteries, EVs and fuel cells to the grid and control their P and Q; FACTS devices (SVC, STATCOM (static synchronous compensator), TCSC (thyristor-controlled series capacitor), UPFC (unified power flow controller)) to control voltage and power flow; HVDC links for long-distance and asynchronous connections; solid-state transformers and circuit breakers; custom power devices (DVR, D-STATCOM, active filters) for power quality.
  • Energy storage: batteries (lithium-ion, lead-acid, flow batteries, sodium-sulphur), pumped hydro, compressed air (CAES), flywheels, supercapacitors, SMES (superconducting magnetic energy storage), hydrogen/thermal storage.
  • Uses of storage: smooth and firm up variable renewables, peak shaving and load levelling, frequency regulation and spinning reserve, voltage support, black start, backup for microgrids and islanding, deferring network upgrades.

Memory trick: Three families = "Talk, Sense-and-Act, Shape-and-Store".

A6 Smart meter, AMR vs AMI, how AMI works, architecture for communication between smart meter and utility server Very likely · 100%Easy

Past-paper questions · Must study

  • 2023 Q3(a) [10] What are the differences between AMR (automatic meter reading) and AMI (advanced metering infrastructure)? How do AMI meters work?
  • 2022 Q3(a) [9] What is a smart meter? Using a diagram, show the typical architecture for communication between a smart meter and the utility server.
  • 2022 Q3(b) [6] What is advanced metering infrastructure (AMI) in smart grid? Write down the differences between AMR and AMI.
  • 2020 Q2(a) [15] Using a diagram show a typical architecture for communication between a smart meter and the utility server.
★ REMEMBER IT
  • AMR (automatic meter reading) = one-way: the meter only sends readings. AMI (advanced metering infrastructure) = two-way: meter ↔ utility, remote connect/disconnect, time-of-use prices, outage alerts, demand response. AMI = smart meters + communication network + meter data management system (MDMS).
Before you start: from meter reader to smart meter

Old way: a meter reader walks to each house every month. AMR (automatic meter reading) lets the utility read the meter remotely, but only one way and mainly for billing.

AMI (advanced metering infrastructure) is a full two-way system: smart meters + communication network + utility software. The utility can also send commands and prices to the meter, and the meter reports outages and power quality.

Smart meter (2022 3a)

A smart meter is an electronic meter that measures and records electricity consumption (and voltage, demand, power factor) at short intervals (15-60 min) and communicates this information two-way with the utility, and often with in-home devices. Parts: metrology chip (measurement), microcontroller with memory and real-time clock, communication modules (NAN and HAN (home area network)), remote connect/disconnect relay, display, tamper sensors, power supply.

Architecture for communication between smart meter and utility server (2022 3a, 2020 2a)
  1. Smart meter measures and stores interval data; talks to home devices over the HAN (ZigBee/Wi-Fi).
  2. NAN (neighbourhood area network) / field area network: meters send data by RF (radio frequency) mesh or PLC (meters can relay each other's data) to a data concentrator (collector) on a pole or substation.
  3. WAN (wide area network) backhaul: the concentrator forwards data over cellular, fibre or WiMAX (Worldwide Interoperability for Microwave Access (IEEE 802.16)) to the utility data centre.
  4. Head-end system (HES): software that manages communication with all meters, collects data, sends commands (connect/disconnect, firmware update, tariff change).
  5. MDMS (meter data management system) (meter data management system): validates, edits and estimates (VEE) and stores the meter data.
  6. Enterprise applications use the data: billing/customer information system (CIS), outage management system (OMS), DMS (distribution management system), demand response, customer web portal and analytics.
AMR vs AMI (2023 3a, 2022 3b)
AMR (automatic meter reading)AMI (advanced metering infrastructure)
One-way communication (meter → utility)Two-way communication (meter ↔ utility)
Mainly automates billing: monthly or daily totalsInterval data (15-60 min), on-demand reads
Walk-by / drive-by or fixed network readingFixed network: meters, NAN, WAN, head-end, MDMS
No remote controlRemote connect/disconnect, load control, firmware upgrade
Flat tariffsTime-of-use, critical-peak, real-time and prepaid pricing; demand response
No outage or power-quality informationOutage and restoration alerts, voltage and PQ monitoring, tamper detection
Customer gets only the billCustomer gets near-real-time usage information (HAN, web)
First step (older technology)Foundation of the smart grid
How AMI meters work (2023 3a)
  1. The metrology circuit samples voltage and current thousands of times per second and computes kWh, kW, kvarh, V, pf.
  2. The microcontroller time-stamps and stores interval readings in memory, applies the active tariff (time of use) and checks for events (outage, tamper, over/under voltage).
  3. At scheduled times (or on request) the communication module sends the data through the NAN to the collector, then via the WAN to the head-end and MDMS.
  4. The utility sends commands back the same way: price signals, demand-response events, remote disconnect/reconnect, firmware updates, prepaid credit.
  5. The meter shares data with home devices through the HAN so consumers and smart appliances can react to prices.
  6. Last-gasp message on power failure tells the OMS (outage management system) exactly where an outage is.

Memory trick: AMR = Automatic Reading (one way); AMI = Advanced, Interactive (two way). Path: "Meter - Mesh - Concentrator - Backhaul - Head-end - MDMS - Billing".

A9 Load flow in smart grids: classical methods, old vs desired load flow, essential features, why needed and challenges Very likely · 100%Easy

Past-paper questions · Must study

  • 2023 Q4(c) [10] Write down the name of the classical methods of load flow solution. What are the essential features of the load flow solution in smart grids?
  • 2022 Q4(b) [10] Make a comparison between the old and desired load flow technique in smart grids.
  • 2020 Q3(a) [10] Why are load flow studies essential in smart grid? Discuss the challenges of load flow in smart grid.
★ REMEMBER IT
  • Classical load flow methods: Gauss-Seidel (simple, slow), Newton-Raphson (fast, accurate, most used), fast decoupled (quick approximation). Smart grids need load flow that handles two-way flow, DG (distributed generation) uncertainty, unbalanced three-phase feeders and real-time updates.
Before you start: what load flow is

Load flow (power flow) is the basic calculation of power system engineering: given the loads (P, Q) and generator outputs, find the voltage magnitude and angle at every bus, and then the power flowing in every line and the losses. It is like solving a big network of non-linear equations, so it is done by iteration.

Smart grids add DG, two-way flows, unbalanced feeders and fast-changing renewables, so the old load-flow methods need upgrading.

Why load flow studies are essential (2020 3a)
  • Planning: size lines, transformers and generators for future loads and DG.
  • Operation: check voltages and line flows are within limits; find losses.
  • Basis for economic dispatch and optimal power flow, contingency analysis and security assessment, stability studies and state estimation.
  • In smart grids: to assess DG/renewable hosting capacity, reverse flows, voltage rise, microgrid operation, EV charging impact and real-time control decisions.
Classical methods of load flow solution (2023 4c)
MethodIdeaFeatures
Gauss-Seidel (GS)Update each bus voltage in turn using the latest values: Vi = (1/Yii)[(Pi − jQi)/Vi* − ΣYijVj]Simple, little memory; slow, many iterations, poor convergence for large systems; uses Ybus
Newton-Raphson (NR)Linearise the power mismatch equations with the Jacobian and solve for corrections [Δδ; Δ|V|] = J−1[ΔP; ΔQ]Quadratic convergence (3-5 iterations), accurate, the industry standard; more computation per iteration
Fast decoupled (FDLF)Uses weak coupling P-δ and Q-V, constant simplified Jacobians (B′, B″)Very fast and memory-efficient; good for real-time and contingency studies; may fail for high R/X
DC load flowLinear, lossless approximation: P = Bδ, |V| = 1Very fast estimate of active flows; used in markets and screening
Old vs desired load flow technique for smart grids (2022 4b) and essential features (2023 4c)
Old (conventional) load flowDesired (smart grid) load flow
Deterministic: fixed load and generation valuesProbabilistic / stochastic: handles uncertain renewables, EVs and loads
Transmission level, balanced single-phase equivalentTransmission + distribution, unbalanced three-phase, radial and meshed
Central generation, one-way flows; DG ignoredDG, storage, microgrids and two-way flows modelled (PV, PQ, droop buses)
Off-line, one snapshotOn-line, real-time, uses PMU (phasor measurement unit)/AMI data; time-series (quasi-dynamic)
Assumes low R/X; methods may diverge on distribution feedersRobust for high R/X feeders (backward-forward sweep, current injection)
Single objective: find stateIntegrated with optimisation (OPF, Volt/VAR), contingency and stability analysis, adaptive/intelligent
Moderate sizeVery large scale; parallel/distributed computing, fast

Essential features of load flow in smart grids: fast and robust convergence; handles unbalanced three-phase distribution and high R/X; models DG, storage, power electronics and microgrid controls; stochastic/probabilistic to deal with intermittency; works in real time with PMU and smart meter data; distributed computation; integrates with optimisation and security tools.

Challenges of load flow in smart grid (2020 3a)
  1. Intermittent, uncertain renewables and EV loads (need probabilistic and time-series studies).
  2. Two-way power flow and voltage rise with DG.
  3. Unbalanced, radial distribution networks with high R/X (NR and FDLF (fast decoupled load flow) may diverge).
  4. Very large size: transmission + distribution + microgrids → heavy computation.
  5. Modelling of inverters, storage and their controls (droop, Q-limits).
  6. Real-time requirements with huge data from AMI (advanced metering infrastructure) and PMUs; data quality and communication delays.
  7. Islanding/microgrid operation without a single slack bus.

Memory trick: Classical = "GS slow, NR strong, Fast Decoupled fast, DC rough". Smart load flow = "Stochastic, Three-phase, DG-aware, Real-time, Robust".

A4 Distributed generation (DG) and microgrid: definition, advantages, configuration, grid-connected and islanded operation Very likely · 83%Easy

Past-paper questions · Must study

  • 2023 Q2(a) [10] Define the term "distributed generation (DG)". What are the advantages of DG (distributed generation)?
  • 2023 Q2(b) [10] Draw the typical configuration of a micro-grid. Describe the grid-connected and islanded operation of the micro-grid.
  • 2022 Q2(a) [11] Define the term "distributed generation (DG)". What are the advantages of DG?
  • 2022 Q3(d) [8] Draw the configuration of a typical microgrid and describe its operation.
LEARN IT FROM ZERO
Distributed generation and microgrids, from zero

Distributed generation (DG) = small generators (kW to a few MW) placed close to the loads, in the distribution network: rooftop PV, small wind, CHP (combined heat and power), fuel cells, diesel sets. Benefits: lower line losses, less transmission needed, better reliability, uses local renewables, faster to build.

A microgrid is a small piece of the grid (a campus, village, factory) with its own DG, storage and loads, and a point of common coupling (PCC) switch to the main grid. Grid-connected mode: the switch is closed; the main grid fixes voltage and frequency and absorbs any surplus or deficit. Islanded mode: on a grid fault the switch opens; now the microgrid's own controllers (and storage) must hold voltage and frequency and shed low-priority loads if needed. When the grid is back, it resynchronises and recloses.

Before you start: small power near the user

Instead of only a few giant power stations far away, many small generators are placed close to where power is used: rooftop solar panels, small wind turbines, biogas or diesel gensets, fuel cells, micro-turbines. That is distributed generation (DG).

Group some DGs, batteries and loads together with their own controller and a switch to the main grid, and you get a microgrid: a small grid that can work with the big grid or alone (islanded) when the big grid fails.

Distributed generation: definition (2023 2a, 2022 2a)

Distributed generation (DG) is electric power generation within distribution networks or on the customer side of the network, close to the point of use, typically from a few kW up to about 50 MW, not centrally planned or dispatched. Technologies: solar PV, wind turbines, small hydro, biomass/biogas, fuel cells, micro-turbines, reciprocating (diesel/gas) engines, combined heat and power (CHP), and storage.

Advantages of DG
  1. Reduced transmission and distribution losses because power is produced near the load.
  2. Improved voltage profile along feeders and better power quality.
  3. Higher reliability: backup supply and islanding (microgrids) during grid outages.
  4. Deferral of investment in new transmission/distribution lines and large plants; relieves congestion.
  5. Uses renewable energy → lower emissions and fuel import; supports climate goals.
  6. High overall efficiency with CHP (waste heat used, up to 80-90 %).
  7. Short installation time, modular, low capital risk; easy to site.
  8. Electrification of remote areas and islands (solar home systems, mini-grids in Bangladesh).
  9. Peak shaving and ancillary services; customer choice and energy independence.

Side note: Challenges of DG: reverse power flow, voltage rise, changes in fault level and protection, islanding safety, harmonics from inverters, intermittency - handled by active distribution management and microgrids.

Microgrid configuration and operation (2023 2b, 2022 3d)

A microgrid is a group of interconnected loads and distributed energy resources (DGs and storage) within clearly defined electrical boundaries that acts as a single controllable entity with respect to the grid and can operate in both grid-connected and island modes.

Components: DG units (PV, wind, micro-turbine, fuel cell, diesel) with power-electronic interfaces; energy storage; critical and non-critical loads; the point of common coupling (PCC) with a static switch (fast thyristor/IGBT switch or breaker) to the utility; microsource controllers (local controllers at each DG) and the microgrid central controller (MGCC) for energy management.

Grid-connected mode: the static switch is closed. The utility grid fixes voltage and frequency; DGs run in constant-power (PQ) mode at their economic/maximum output; surplus is exported and deficits imported; storage charges or shaves peaks; the microgrid can sell power and provide services (demand response, reactive power).

Islanded (autonomous) mode: when a fault or poor power quality is detected on the utility side, the static switch opens within a few cycles and the microgrid separates. Now it must create its own voltage and frequency: one or more DGs/storage inverters switch to voltage-frequency (V/f) control or droop control (frequency falls slightly as load rises, so units share load); storage covers the sudden mismatch; non-critical loads are shed if generation is insufficient so that critical loads (hospitals, control rooms) stay supplied. When the grid recovers, the MGCC (microgrid central controller) resynchronises (matches voltage, frequency, phase) and recloses the static switch.

Memory trick: DG advantages = "Less Loss, Better Voltage, More Reliability, Defer Investment, Green". Microgrid: PCC (point of common coupling) + static switch + DGs + storage + loads + MGCC; PQ mode on-grid, V/f droop off-grid.

A7 Demand side management (DSM): load shifting, valley filling, peak clipping (load-shape curves) Very likely · 83%Easy

Past-paper questions · Must study

  • 2023 Q3(b) [15] What is meant by demand side management? Describe how the following techniques modify the load consumption patterns: (i) load shifting, (ii) valley filling, (iii) peak clipping.
  • 2022 Q3(c) [12] What is meant by demand side management? Describe how the following techniques modify the load consumption patterns: (i) load shifting, (ii) valley filling, (iii) peak clipping.
LEARN IT FROM ZERO
Demand side management, from zero

Building a power plant just to cover the evening peak is very expensive. Instead, demand side management (DSM) changes when and how much customers use, so the daily load curve becomes flatter. The classic load-shape objectives:

  • Peak clipping: cut load at the peak (utility switches off water heaters/ACs for a while). Peak goes down, energy goes down a little.
  • Valley filling: add load at night when demand is low (EV charging, ice storage). Valley comes up, energy goes up.
  • Load shifting: move load from the peak to the valley (run washing machines at night with time-of-use tariffs). Same energy, flatter curve.
  • Others: strategic conservation (efficiency, less energy everywhere), strategic load growth, flexible load shape.

Move the sliders: the shaded curve is the original, the coloured one is after DSM (demand side management).

Interactive graph (needs JavaScript; open the HTML version).

Before you start: shaping the load curve

The load curve (power demand vs hour of the day) has a tall evening peak and a deep night valley. The utility must build enough plants for the peak, which then sit idle most of the day - very expensive.

DSM (demand side management) changes when and how much customers use, so the curve becomes flatter. Think of six shapes: cut the top, fill the bottom, move load from top to bottom, use less overall, add useful load, or keep load flexible.

Demand side management (2023 3b, 2022 3c)

Demand side management (DSM) is the planning, implementation and monitoring of utility activities designed to influence customers' use of electricity in ways that produce desired changes in the utility's load shape - the time pattern and magnitude of demand. Tools: tariffs (time-of-use, critical-peak, real-time pricing), direct load control, interruptible contracts, energy-efficiency programmes, storage and smart appliances, all made practical by smart meters and AMI (advanced metering infrastructure). Benefits: lower peak, less need for peaking plants and network upgrades, lower cost and emissions, better reliability, and lower bills for customers.

TechniqueHow it modifies the load curveMeansEffect
(i) Load shiftingMoves load from peak hours to off-peak hours; total energy about the sameTime-of-use tariffs; thermal (ice/water) storage; scheduling washing machines, pumps, EV charging, industrial processes at night; battery storageLower peak AND filled valley; flatter curve; best use of base-load plants
(ii) Valley fillingBuilds load in off-peak periods (night) onlyCheap night tariffs; EV charging at night; off-peak water heating and pumping; charging storageRaises the valley and the load factor; lowers average cost of supply since spare base capacity is used
(iii) Peak clippingReduces load only during peak hoursDirect load control (utility switches off air-conditioners, water heaters, pumps for short periods); interruptible tariffs; demand response events; critical-peak pricingCuts the peak demand, avoids building/running costly peaking plants; total energy reduced slightly
Strategic conservationReduces load at all hoursEfficient appliances, LED lighting, insulationWhole curve lower
Strategic load growthIncreases load in a planned wayElectrification (EVs, heat pumps, induction cooking)Whole curve higher but well-utilised
Flexible load shapeLoad can be varied when neededContracts with flexible customers, smart appliancesReliability tool

Memory trick: Clip the top, Fill the bottom, Shift top to bottom.

A2 Active vs passive distribution network; active distribution management scheme (block diagram) Very likely · 83%Easy

Past-paper questions · Must study

  • 2023 Q1(b) [10] What are the differences between an active and a passive distribution network? Draw the block diagram of an active distribution system and describe its operation.
  • 2022 Q1(a) [15] What are the differences between an active and a passive distribution network? Describe the operation of an active distribution management scheme with necessary block diagrams.
UNDERSTAND Read this to understand; you do not need to write it

A passive distribution network only delivers power one way from the substation to loads; nothing is controlled after the feeder breaker. Once DG (rooftop solar, small generators) is connected, power can flow backwards and voltages can rise, so the network must become active: it measures, communicates and controls generators, loads, tap changers and storage in real time from a distribution management system (DMS).

Before you start: passive vs active

A passive distribution network is like a one-way street: power comes from the substation and flows down radial feeders to loads. Designed once with the worst case and then left alone ("fit and forget").

An active network has generators (rooftop PV, wind, CHP (combined heat and power)), storage and controllable loads on the feeders, so power can flow back up. It must therefore be watched and steered continuously, like traffic control on a two-way road.

Active vs passive distribution network (2023 1b, 2022 1a)
Passive distribution networkActive distribution network
No (or negligible) generation; only loadsHas DG (distributed generation), storage, EVs, controllable loads
Unidirectional power flow (substation → loads)Bidirectional power flow
Voltage falls along the feeder; fixed tap and capacitor settingsVoltage can rise near DG; needs coordinated, dynamic voltage control
"Fit and forget" planning for worst caseReal-time monitoring, control and optimisation
Simple overcurrent protection (radial)Adaptive protection (fault current from DG, two-way flows), anti-islanding
Little communication and measurementExtensive sensors, communication, SCADA (supervisory control and data acquisition)/DMS
Consumers passiveConsumers active (prosumers, demand response)
Low DG hosting capacityHigher DG hosting capacity, better asset use
Block diagram and operation of an active distribution management scheme

Operation (a closed control loop that repeats every few seconds to minutes):

  1. Measure: RTUs, IEDs, smart meters, PMUs and sensors measure voltages, currents, power flows, switch status, DG output at substations and along feeders.
  2. Communicate: data go through the SCADA / distribution automation network to the distribution management system (DMS) in the control centre.
  3. Estimate and forecast: distribution state estimation fills gaps in the measurements and gives the complete network state; load and DG (solar/wind) output are forecast.
  4. Decide (control functions): coordinated voltage/VAR control (on-load tap changer, capacitors, DG reactive power); DG dispatch or curtailment and storage scheduling; network reconfiguration to reduce losses or relieve overloads; demand response; fault location, isolation and service restoration (FLISR, self-healing); protection setting adaptation.
  5. Act: commands are sent back to tap changers, switches, DG inverters, storage and controllable loads.
  6. The new state is measured again, closing the loop. Operators supervise through the HMI (human-machine interface).

Side note: The control can be centralised (one DMS (distribution management system) decides), decentralised (local controllers at DGs and substations) or hierarchical (local + central), and in research also by multi-agent systems (A11).

Memory trick: Active network loop: "Measure - Send - Estimate - Decide - Act". Passive = "fit and forget".

A5 Smart grid communication: SCADA, HAN/NAN/WAN, and where Bluetooth, ZigBee, WLAN, WPAN and WiMAX are used Very likely · 100%Medium

Past-paper questions · Must study

  • 2023 Q2(c) [15] What is meant by SCADA (supervisory control and data acquisition)? What are the advantages of a SCADA integrated system? Show the possible communication infrastructure for the smart grid including HAN (home area network), NAN (neighbourhood area network) and WAN (wide area network).
  • 2022 Q2(c) [12] Define HAN, NAN and WAN. Compare the conventional and smart meter. Write down the application areas of the following communication technologies in smart grid: Bluetooth, WiMAX (Worldwide Interoperability for Microwave Access (IEEE 802.16)) and WLAN (wireless local area network (Wi-Fi)).
  • 2020 Q2(b) [15] Write down the application areas of the following communication technologies in smart grid: Bluetooth, ZigBee, WLAN, WPAN (wireless personal area network), WiMAX.
★ REMEMBER IT
  • Network sizes: HAN (home area: ZigBee, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth; metres) → NAN (neighbourhood: meters to collector; RF (radio frequency) mesh, PLC, WiMAX; hundreds of m to km) → WAN (utility backbone: fibre, cellular, WiMAX; tens of km).
  • Where each fits: Bluetooth = very short (meter to phone); ZigBee = low power home devices and meters; WLAN = home/substation LAN; WPAN = personal devices; WiMAX = long range NAN/WAN backhaul.
  • SCADA = Supervisory Control And Data Acquisition: RTUs in substations send data to the control centre; operators supervise and switch remotely.
Before you start: how the grid talks

SCADA (supervisory control and data acquisition) is the classic remote-control system of a utility: little computers in the field (RTUs) read meters and switch positions, send them over a network to a master station, and the operator can open/close breakers from the control room.

Smart grid communication is organised by distance, like phone networks: HAN inside one home, NAN across a neighbourhood, WAN across the country to the utility.

SCADA and its advantages (2023 2c)

SCADA is a computer-based system that gathers real-time data from remote field devices, presents it to operators and lets them control equipment remotely. Components: field devices (sensors, CTs/PTs, breakers), RTUs (remote terminal units) / IEDs / PLCs that acquire data and execute commands, a communication network (fibre, radio, PLC, cellular), and the master station (MTU) with servers, historian database and HMI (human-machine interface) (human-machine interface) screens. Functions: data acquisition, monitoring and alarms, supervisory control, data logging, trending; EMS (energy management system)/DMS applications run on top.

Advantages of a SCADA-integrated system:

  1. Real-time monitoring of the whole network from one place; faster fault detection and alarms.
  2. Remote control of breakers, tap changers, capacitors → fewer site visits and staff.
  3. Faster restoration after faults, less outage time (higher reliability indices).
  4. Better efficiency: economic dispatch, loss reduction, voltage control via EMS/DMS.
  5. Historical data for planning, maintenance and analysis; condition monitoring.
  6. Improved safety of personnel and equipment.
  7. Integration with smart grid applications (AMI, DMS (distribution management system), OMS (outage management system), WAMS (wide area monitoring system)).
HAN, NAN and WAN (2023 2c, 2022 2c)
NetworkMeaning and coverageConnectsTechnologies
HAN (home area network)Inside a home/building; ~10-100 m; low data rateSmart meter, smart appliances, thermostats, in-home display, EV charger, rooftop PVZigBee, Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, HomePlug (PLC), Z-Wave
NAN (neighbourhood area network; also FAN (field area network), field area network)A neighbourhood or feeder; ~1-10 kmMany smart meters to a data concentrator/collector; distribution automation devicesRF mesh, Wi-Fi mesh, PLC, WiMAX, cellular
WAN (wide area network)Utility-wide backbone; 10-100+ km; high data rateCollectors, substations and power plants to control centresOptical fibre, WiMAX, cellular LTE (Long Term Evolution (4G cellular))/5G, microwave, satellite
Conventional meter vs smart meter (2022 2c)

Application areas of communication technologies (2022 2c, 2020 2b)
TechnologyWhat it isSmart grid applications

Memory trick: Distance ladder: HAN home < NAN neighbourhood < WAN wide. Technologies: "Blue and Zig at home, Wi-Fi in the building, WiMAX across the town".
