  • 2020 Q3(b) [20] Provide an overview of the following performance analysis tools for smart grid design: (i) DSOPF (dynamic stochastic optimal power flow), (ii) SSA (static security assessment), (iii) congestion, (iv) contingency.
★ REMEMBER IT
  • Contingency analysis = "what if line X or generator Y trips?" (N−1). SCOPF (security-constrained optimal power flow) = optimal power flow that also stays safe for every listed contingency. DSOPF = dynamic stochastic OPF (handles uncertainty over time). SSA = static security assessment: checks voltage and line limits after each contingency. Congestion = a line is at its limit, so cheaper power cannot reach the load.
Before you start: checking the grid is safe and cheap

A grid must survive the sudden loss of any one line or generator (the N-1 rule). Contingency analysis asks "what if this element trips?" for every element. Security assessment uses these answers to say whether the present state is safe.

Optimal power flow (OPF) finds the cheapest generator settings that respect all limits. Make it respect the limits after contingencies too and it is security-constrained OPF (optimal power flow).

N-1 means: with N elements, the system must still be OK with any one (1) of them out.

Contingency analysis and why it is important (2023 4a, 2020 3b)

Contingency analysis is the study of the effect of the outage of a component (line, transformer, generator) on the power system: for each credible contingency it runs a (fast) load flow and checks for line overloads, voltage violations and islanding. Contingencies are screened and ranked by severity indices so that only critical ones are studied in detail.

  • Ensures the system remains secure (N-1, N-2) and prevents cascading outages and blackouts.
  • Tells operators which outages are dangerous and what preventive or corrective actions (re-dispatch, switching, load shedding) are needed.
  • Basis for security assessment, SCOPF, transmission planning and maintenance scheduling.
  • In smart grids, needed more often (in real time) because renewables and two-way flows change conditions quickly.
Security-constrained optimal power flow (SCOPF) with example (2023 4a)

OPF minimises an objective (generation cost or losses) subject to the power flow equations and limits (generator P, Q limits, bus voltage limits, line thermal limits). SCOPF adds the constraints of each credible contingency: the chosen operating point must keep all flows and voltages within (emergency) limits not only in the base case but also after any single contingency (preventive SCOPF), or must be correctable by allowed post-contingency actions (corrective SCOPF).

min ΣCi(PGi) subject to: g0(x0, u) = 0, h0(x0, u) ≤ 0 (base case); gk(xk, u) = 0, hk(xk, u) ≤ 0 for every contingency k

Example: two generators feed a load centre of 300 MW through two parallel lines of 200 MW rating each. The cheap generator G1 (Tk 3/kWh) is at the far end, the costly G2 (Tk 8/kWh) at the load centre. Plain OPF sends all 300 MW from G1 through the two lines (150 MW each). If one line trips, the other must carry 300 MW > 200 MW → overload and cascading outage. SCOPF limits G1 so that the remaining line carries ≤ 200 MW after the trip: G1 = 200 MW and G2 = 100 MW. The cost is higher, but the system stays secure under N-1.

Static security assessment (SSA) (2022 4c, 2020 3b)

SSA evaluates whether the power system, in its steady state after a contingency, will operate within all limits (line flows, bus voltages, generator limits) - ignoring the transient swings in between. Steps: (1) obtain the present state from state estimation; (2) select a list of credible contingencies; (3) run contingency (load flow) analysis for each; (4) check limit violations and compute severity indices; (5) classify the system as secure (normal), alert/insecure (a contingency would cause violation) or emergency; (6) suggest preventive/corrective control. In smart grids, SSA must be fast (using PMU (phasor measurement unit) data, DC/decoupled load flow, AI/pattern recognition) because conditions change rapidly.

DSOPF (2020 3b)

DSOPF (dynamic stochastic optimal power flow), proposed by Momoh for smart grids, extends OPF to handle time (dynamic: the decision now affects future states) and uncertainty (stochastic: random loads, renewable output, outages). It combines OPF with adaptive dynamic programming / approximate dynamic programming so the optimiser learns and adapts in real time. Uses: optimal dispatch with renewables and storage, adaptive Volt/VAR control, reconfiguration, demand response, self-healing and resilient operation. Advantages: predictive, adaptive, handles variable resources; disadvantage: heavy computation.

Congestion (2020 3b)

Congestion occurs when a transmission line or transformer reaches its thermal, voltage or stability limit, so the desired (cheapest) power transfers cannot all be made. Congestion management: re-dispatch of generation (out-of-merit), FACTS (flexible AC transmission systems) and phase-shifting transformers to re-route flows, demand response and storage at the receiving end, locational marginal pricing and congestion charges/financial transmission rights in markets, network reinforcement, dynamic line rating. Smart grid tools (PMUs, DLR (dynamic line rating) sensors, DSM (demand side management)) relieve congestion at lower cost.

Necessity of GIS and Google mapping tools in smart grids (2023 4b)
  • Show every asset (poles, lines, transformers, meters, DGs) on a map with its attributes: an accurate network model for load flow and DMS (distribution management system).
  • Outage management: locate faults and affected customers on the map; dispatch the nearest crew with the best route.
  • Planning: route new lines, site DG (distributed generation)/solar and substations considering land, terrain, flood zones.
  • Vegetation management, asset maintenance and theft detection.
  • Visualising real-time data (loads, outages, EV chargers) for operators and customers; emergency/disaster response.

Memory trick: Contingency = "what if one trips?"; SSA = "are we safe after it?"; SCOPF = cheapest that is still safe; DSOPF = OPF + time + uncertainty; congestion = traffic jam on lines.

A8 Phasor measurement unit (PMU) and synchronised phasor measuring system (WAMS) Very likely · 83%Medium

Past-paper questions · Must study

  • 2023 Q3(c) [10] What are the key features of a phasor measurement unit (PMU)? Explain the operation of a PMU (phasor measurement unit) with necessary block diagrams.
  • 2022 Q4(a) [10] What is a phasor measurement unit in smart grid? Discuss a synchronized phasor measuring system with conceptual diagram.
UNDERSTAND Read this to understand; you do not need to write it

A PMU (phasor measurement unit) measures voltage and current phasors (magnitude and angle) 30–60 times a second, each stamped with GPS (Global Positioning System) time to within a microsecond. Because all PMUs share the same clock, a control centre can line up angles from stations hundreds of km apart and see the whole grid's state at once (a synchrophasor or wide-area measurement system, WAMS (wide area monitoring system)).

Block diagram to draw: CT/PT input → anti-aliasing filter → A/D converter (sampling clock locked to GPS via phase-locked oscillator) → phasor microprocessor (DFT) → time-stamped output → communication → PDC (phasor data concentrator) → control centre.

Before you start: measuring the grid's heartbeat in sync

AC voltage is a sine wave; a phasor describes it by its size (magnitude) and its position in time (phase angle). Comparing phase angles at two far-apart substations tells you how stressed the grid between them is (bigger angle difference = more power flowing, closer to instability).

But to compare angles, both measurements must be taken at exactly the same moment. A PMU uses GPS satellite time (accurate to 1 microsecond) to time-stamp every measurement, so measurements from the whole country can be lined up. Old SCADA (supervisory control and data acquisition) gives one slow, unsynchronised reading every 2-4 seconds; a PMU gives 30-60 synchronised readings per second.

PMU: definition and key features (2023 3c, 2022 4a)

A phasor measurement unit (PMU) is a device that measures the voltage and current phasors (magnitude and phase angle), frequency and rate of change of frequency (ROCOF) at a bus, synchronised to a common time source (GPS), and streams them as time-stamped synchrophasors (IEEE C37.118 standard).

  • GPS time synchronisation (1 μs accuracy; 1 μs = 0.018° at 50 Hz), so angles from different locations are directly comparable.
  • High reporting rate: 25/50 frames per second at 50 Hz (30/60 at 60 Hz) vs 2-4 s for SCADA - captures dynamics and oscillations.
  • Measures positive-sequence voltage and current phasors, frequency, ROCOF (rate of change of frequency), also individual phases.
  • Direct measurement of the phase angle (SCADA cannot measure angles; state estimation had to calculate them).
  • High accuracy (total vector error < 1 %), standard data format, can be stand-alone or built into relays/recorders.
  • Enables wide-area monitoring, protection and control (WAMPAC).
Operation of a PMU (block diagram)
  1. Analog inputs: three-phase voltages and currents from potential and current transformers (PT/CT).
  2. Anti-aliasing filters remove frequencies above half the sampling rate so the digital samples are correct.
  3. A/D converter (16-bit) samples the waveforms; the sampling clock comes from a phase-locked oscillator locked to the GPS receiver's one-pulse-per-second (1 PPS (pulse per second)) signal, so every PMU samples at the same instants.
  4. Phasor microprocessor computes the phasor of each signal with a recursive DFT (discrete Fourier transform) over one cycle, then the positive-sequence phasor, frequency and ROCOF.
  5. Each result is time-stamped with the GPS time (UTC).
  6. The modem/communication module sends the data frames to a PDC (phasor data concentrator).
Synchronised phasor measuring system / WAMS (2022 4a)

PMUs at many substations send data to local PDCs (phasor data concentrators), which align measurements with the same time stamp, check quality and forward them to a super PDC at the control centre. Applications use the coherent snapshot of the whole grid: wide-area visualisation (angle differences across the network), real-time monitoring of oscillations and voltage stability, improved state estimation (direct linear estimation), post-disturbance analysis, model validation, adaptive and wide-area protection, islanding detection, and control of FACTS (flexible AC transmission systems)/HVDC.

Memory trick: PMU = "GPS + Filter + A/D + DFT (discrete Fourier transform) + Time stamp + Send". WAMS = PMUs → PDC → super PDC → applications.

A11 Multi-agent systems (MAS): IDAPS and decentralised meter reading Very likely · 83%Medium

Past-paper questions · Must study

  • 2023 Q4(d) [10] Design a decentralized meter reading system using the multi-agent approach.
  • 2022 Q4(d) [10] What is meant by a multi-agent system (MAS)? Develop an intelligent distributed autonomous power system (IDAPS) using the MAS (multi-agent system) approach.
UNDERSTAND Read this to understand; you do not need to write it

A multi-agent system is a team of small software programs (agents), each with its own job and a bit of intelligence, that talk to each other to reach a goal without one central boss. In IDAPS (intelligent distributed autonomous power system) you would have a control agent (watches the grid, detects outages), DER (distributed energy resource) agent (controls each generator/storage), user agent (each customer's loads and preferences) and database agent (stores data). On a grid fault they island the area and keep critical loads supplied by themselves.

Before you start: many small brains instead of one big one

In a multi-agent system (MAS) each part of the grid (a DG (distributed generation), a load, a meter) gets its own small software "agent" that can see its local situation, decide and act by itself, and chat with other agents. Together they solve the problem without one central computer. If one agent fails, the others continue: no single point of failure.

Multi-agent system (2022 4d)

An agent is a software (or hardware) entity situated in an environment that is autonomous (acts without direct human control), reactive (senses and responds to changes), pro-active (pursues its goals) and social (communicates and cooperates with other agents). A multi-agent system (MAS) is a group of such agents that interact (through messages in an agent communication language such as FIPA-ACL, on platforms like JADE (Java Agent DEvelopment framework)) to achieve goals that are beyond any single agent. Advantages for smart grids: distributed and scalable, flexible (plug-and-play DG), robust to failures, fast local decisions, suits distributed resources and microgrids.

IDAPS (intelligent distributed autonomous power system) using the MAS approach (2022 4d)

IDAPS (intelligent distributed autonomous power system) is a microgrid concept (Virginia Tech, Rahman et al.) in which distributed energy resources and loads in a neighbourhood are managed by a multi-agent system so that the area can supply itself, trade energy and island during an upstream outage to keep critical loads supplied.

AgentFunction
Control agentMonitors voltage and frequency at the point of connection; detects upstream faults/outages; decides to island the microgrid (opens the main breaker) and to reconnect when the grid is normal; sends signals to the other agents
DER agentStores information on each DER (type, rating, availability, cost); monitors and controls its output (start, stop, set-point); offers energy and bids in the local market
User (load) agentRepresents customers; monitors loads, knows which are critical; sheds or reschedules non-critical loads during islanding or high prices (demand response)
Database agentStores system data, agent directory and history; provides information to other agents

Operation: in normal conditions DER agents and user agents trade and schedule energy. When the control agent detects a fault upstream (e.g. voltage sag), it sends "island" messages: the main switch opens, the DER agents ramp up generation and storage, the user agent sheds non-critical loads so that critical loads remain supplied; when the grid recovers, the control agent re-synchronises and reconnects. The design steps: (1) define the system and objectives; (2) identify agents and their roles; (3) define their knowledge and behaviour (rules); (4) define message types and communication (FIPA-ACL, JADE platform); (5) implement and test by simulation.

Decentralised meter reading system using the multi-agent approach (2023 4d)
  1. Meter agents (one in each smart meter): measure and store interval consumption, detect tamper and outages, respond to read requests, and push data autonomously at scheduled times; can relay neighbours' messages (mesh).
  2. Collector agents (one per feeder/area, in data concentrators): discover and register meter agents in their area, poll or receive readings, validate (check missing/abnormal values), aggregate, and forward to the upper level. Neighbouring collectors back each other up if one fails - no single point of failure.
  3. Directory/database agent: keeps the registry of all agents and stores meter data (like an MDMS (meter data management system)).
  4. Billing agent: applies tariffs (time-of-use, prepaid) to the data and generates bills; sends price signals back to meter agents.
  5. Monitoring agent: analyses data for outages, theft (comparing feeder energy with sum of meters), voltage problems and demand-response events.
  6. Agents communicate by standard messages (request, inform, agree, failure) over the NAN (neighbourhood area network)/WAN; new meters join by registering - plug and play.

Advantages: scalable to millions of meters, robust, reduced traffic (local aggregation), fast local decisions (outage detection), easy expansion.

Memory trick: Agent = "Autonomous, Reactive, Pro-active, Social". IDAPS agents = "Control, DER, User, Database".

Section B: Power system control and stability, power quality, intelligence, security, renewables

Sort Section B:

B8 Computational intelligence and decision tools: ANN, expert systems, AHP, decision support tools, stability tools and computational challenges Very likely · 100%Easy

Past-paper questions · Must study

  • 2023 Q7(b) [10] What is meant by ANN (artificial neural network)? How does the ANN facilitate the assessment of smart grid performance?
  • 2023 Q8(b) [10] How do expert systems (ES) enhance decision-making and operational efficiency in smart grid? Discuss.
  • 2022 Q7(b) [10] How can decision support tools be used in smart grid planning and operations? Describe.
  • 2022 Q7(c) [10] What is the role of the Analytical Hierarchical Programming (AHP) method in smart grid management? Explain with necessary block diagram.
  • 2022 Q8(d) [12] Describe the computational challenges faced by researchers and engineers for the design, planning and operations of smart power system.
  • 2020 Q5(a) [10] What are the stability analysis tools for smart grid? Write the reasons of computational challenges in smart grids.
  • 2020 Q5(c) [10] How does an Artificial Neural Network (ANN) improve smart grid technology? Illustrate the Analytical Hierarchical Programming (AHP) method.
★ REMEMBER IT
  • ANN = learns from past data (load and price forecasting, fault detection). Expert system = rules from human experts (if-then) for diagnosis and restoration. AHP (analytical hierarchy process (the paper calls it analytical hierarchical programming)) = compare options pair-wise against weighted criteria to rank them (choose a site, a technology).
Before you start: making the grid think

The smart grid produces huge amounts of data and must make decisions quickly under uncertainty. Computational intelligence tools help: ANN learns patterns from past data like a brain; expert systems store experts' rules (IF ... THEN ...); AHP helps choose between options by comparing criteria two at a time; decision support tools combine these with data and models to advise planners and operators.

ANN and how it facilitates assessment of smart grid performance (2023 7b, 2020 5c)

An artificial neural network (ANN) is a computational model inspired by the brain, made of interconnected neurons arranged in layers (input, hidden, output). Each neuron forms a weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias and passes it through an activation function (sigmoid, ReLU). The network is trained on example data (e.g. back-propagation adjusts the weights to minimise error), after which it can map new inputs to outputs very fast, handle non-linear relationships and noisy data, and generalise.

Uses in the smart grid:

  • Load and price forecasting (short-term, from weather, time, history).
  • Renewable forecasting (solar irradiance, wind power).
  • Security and stability assessment: classify operating states as secure/insecure quickly instead of running many load flows; voltage stability margin estimation.
  • Fault detection, classification and location from waveforms; PQ disturbance classification.
  • State estimation and bad-data/false-data detection; non-technical loss (theft) detection from meter data.
  • Control: adaptive controllers for FACTS (flexible AC transmission systems), microgrids, EV charging, demand response.
Expert systems (2023 8b)

An expert system (ES) is a computer program that captures the knowledge of human experts as rules (IF-THEN) in a knowledge base and uses an inference engine (forward/backward chaining) with a working memory to reason about a situation and give advice with explanations through a user interface.

  • Alarm processing: during a disturbance hundreds of alarms appear; the ES filters and identifies the root cause.
  • Fault diagnosis and protection analysis from relay and breaker data.
  • Service restoration: plans switching sequences quickly after outages (self-healing).
  • Voltage/VAR control advice, security assessment, maintenance scheduling, operator training.
  • Benefits: consistent fast decisions, stores scarce expertise, reduces operator errors and outage time, improves efficiency. Limits: knowledge acquisition is hard, cannot learn by itself (combine with ANN/fuzzy logic).
Decision support tools in planning and operations (2022 7b)

Decision support tools (DST) integrate data (SCADA, PMU (phasor measurement unit), AMI (advanced metering infrastructure), GIS (geographic information system), weather), models (load flow, OPF (optimal power flow), stability), optimisation and AI with visualisation to help humans decide.

  • Planning: load and DG (distributed generation) forecasting, siting and sizing DG/storage, network expansion, reliability and cost-benefit studies, scenario analysis, multi-criteria choice (AHP).
  • Operations: real-time visualisation (dashboards, GIS), contingency and security assessment, OPF/dispatch, Volt/VAR optimisation, outage management and restoration, demand response scheduling, alarm processing, what-if simulations.
  • Benefits: faster and better-informed decisions, handling of uncertainty, reduced risk and cost.
AHP method (2022 7c, 2020 5c)

The analytical hierarchy process (AHP) (Saaty) is a multi-criteria decision-making method. Role in smart grid management: choosing among investment options (AMI vs storage vs microgrid), ranking DG sites, selecting communication technology or vendors, prioritising projects, evaluating smart grid maturity.

  1. Build the hierarchy: goal at the top, criteria (cost, reliability, environment, security...) in the middle, alternatives at the bottom.
  2. Pairwise comparison of criteria using Saaty's 1-9 scale (1 = equal, 9 = extremely more important) → comparison matrix A (aji = 1/aij).
  3. Priority weights = normalised principal eigenvector of A (or average of normalised columns).
  4. Consistency check: CI = (λmax − n)/(n − 1), CR = CI/RI; accept if CR < 0.1.
  5. Repeat pairwise comparisons of alternatives under each criterion.
  6. Synthesis: overall score of each alternative = Σ(criterion weight × alternative weight); highest score is chosen.
Stability analysis tools and computational challenges (2020 5a, 2022 8d)

Stability analysis tools: time-domain simulation (transient stability programs), equal area criterion, small-signal (eigenvalue/modal) analysis, P-V/Q-V curves and continuation power flow, voltage stability indices, direct (Lyapunov/energy function) methods, PMU-based real-time monitoring (WAMS), and AI-based security assessment (ANN, decision trees).

Computational challenges for design, planning and operation:

  1. Size and complexity: millions of nodes (transmission + distribution + customer devices), many control loops.
  2. Uncertainty: variable renewables, EVs, prices, customer behaviour → stochastic optimisation and many scenarios.
  3. Real-time requirements: decisions in seconds with huge data streams from PMUs and AMI (big data, latency).
  4. Non-linear, multi-objective, mixed-integer optimisation (OPF with switching, unit commitment, reconfiguration).
  5. Multi-time-scale dynamics: power electronics (μs) to markets (hours), low inertia.
  6. Distributed control and communication coordination; data quality, missing data and cyber attacks.
  7. Modelling of new devices (inverters, storage, loads), lack of validated models; integration of different software and standards (interoperability).
  8. Need for high-performance, parallel and cloud computing, and skilled people.

Memory trick: ANN learns, ES reasons by rules, AHP ranks by pairwise comparison, DST combines all for humans. AHP steps: "Hierarchy, Pairwise, Weights, Consistency, Synthesis".

B9 Interoperability and cyber security: threats, false data injection attacks, mitigation Very likely · 100%Easy

Past-paper questions · Must study

  • 2023 Q7(c) [13] What is interoperability in smart grid environment? How can false data injection impact the stability and reliability of smart grid operations, and what measures can be taken to mitigate these risks effectively?
  • 2022 Q7(d) [7] Explain why cyber security is of prime importance in smart grids and how the risk of cyber-attack can be mitigated.
  • 2020 Q6(a) [12] What is interoperability in smart grid environment? How is cyber security a threat to smart grids?
  • 2020 Q6(b) [12] What is false data injection attack in the smart grid? (AGC part in B2)
  • 2020 Q6(c) [6] What are the main mitigation approaches to cyber security risk?
UNDERSTAND Read this to understand; you do not need to write it

Interoperability = devices and systems from different makers can exchange data and work together (common standards: IEC (International Electrotechnical Commission) 61850, DNP3 (Distributed Network Protocol 3), IEC 61968/61970). False data injection: an attacker changes meter or PMU (phasor measurement unit) readings so that the state estimator believes a wrong grid state without raising a bad-data alarm; operators then dispatch wrongly, overload lines or shed load. Mitigation: encryption and authentication, secure PMUs at key buses, anomaly detection, network segmentation, firewalls, training, regular audits.

Before you start: plugging the grid into the internet

A smart grid connects millions of meters, sensors and controllers by networks. That brings two new problems: (1) devices from different makers must understand each other - interoperability; (2) every connected device is a door that a hacker might open - cyber security.

The three goals of cyber security are CIA (confidentiality, integrity, availability): Confidentiality (no one reads what they should not), Integrity (no one changes data), Availability (the system keeps working). In the grid, availability and integrity matter most.

Interoperability (2023 7c, 2020 6a)

Interoperability is the capability of two or more networks, systems, devices, applications or components to exchange information securely and effectively and to use the information exchanged, with little or no inconvenience to the user (NIST/IEEE 2030). It requires common standards for communication protocols, data models and interfaces: IEC 61850 (substation automation), IEC 61968/61970 CIM (common information model), DNP3, IEC 60870-5, IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) C37.118 (PMU), ANSI (American National Standards Institute) C12 and DLMS (Device Language Message Specification)/COSEM (metering), OpenADR (demand response), IEEE 2030. Benefits: plug-and-play devices, vendor competition and lower cost, easier integration and upgrades, protection of investments, better security.

Why cyber security is of prime importance; how it threatens smart grids (2022 7d, 2020 6a)
  • The grid is critical infrastructure: an attack can cause blackouts affecting hospitals, water, transport, economy and national security (e.g. Ukraine 2015/2016 grid attacks, Stuxnet).
  • Huge attack surface: millions of smart meters, IEDs, DG (distributed generation) inverters, EV chargers and wireless links, many in unprotected public places.
  • Two-way communication and remote control (connect/disconnect, set-points) can be misused to switch off loads or destabilise the grid.
  • Legacy SCADA (supervisory control and data acquisition) protocols were designed without security; IT-OT convergence brings internet threats into control systems.
  • Privacy: detailed meter data reveal customers' habits.
  • Threats: malware/ransomware, denial-of-service (blocks AMI (advanced metering infrastructure)/SCADA communication), man-in-the-middle, spoofing, eavesdropping, meter tampering and energy theft, insider attacks, false data injection, GPS (Global Positioning System) spoofing of PMUs.
False data injection (FDI) attacks: impact and mitigation (2023 7c, 2020 6b)

The control centre estimates the system state x from measurements z = Hx + e (H = measurement Jacobian) and uses a residual test to reject bad data. In a false data injection attack, an attacker who knows the network model adds a carefully designed vector a = Hc to the measurements; the estimated state becomes x + c but the residual is unchanged, so the bad-data detector does not notice.

Impact on stability and reliability: operators and EMS (energy management system) see a false picture of the grid; wrong economic dispatch and OPF (optimal power flow) decisions; hidden line overloads or fake congestion leading to tripping and cascading failures; wrong AGC (automatic generation control)/voltage control actions that may cause frequency or voltage instability; manipulated market prices for profit; masking of real faults or physical attacks; energy theft through meter data.

Mitigation: protect a strategically chosen set of key measurements (secured meters, encrypted channels) so that undetectable attack vectors cannot be built; deploy PMUs (independent, GPS-time-stamped measurements); authentication and digital signatures, encryption of measurement data; advanced detection (statistical/consistency checks, machine-learning anomaly detection, comparing with forecasts); keep the network model (H) confidential; moving-target defence (changing system parameters); redundancy.

Main mitigation approaches to cyber security risk (2022 7d, 2020 6c)
  1. Risk assessment and security policy: identify assets, threats and vulnerabilities; follow standards (NISTIR 7628, NERC (North American Electric Reliability Corporation) CIP (critical infrastructure protection), IEC 62351, IEC 62443).
  2. Defence in depth: network segmentation, firewalls, DMZ (demilitarised zone (buffer network)) between IT and OT (operational technology), intrusion detection/prevention systems.
  3. Strong authentication and access control: role-based access, multi-factor authentication, key management.
  4. Encryption and integrity protection of communications (IEC 62351, TLS (Transport Layer Security), VPN (virtual private network)), secure protocols.
  5. Secure devices: tamper-resistant meters, secure firmware updates, patch management, disabling unused services.
  6. Continuous monitoring, logging, anomaly detection and a security operations centre.
  7. Incident response and recovery plans, backups, drills, resilient (islandable) design.
  8. Training and awareness of staff; supply-chain security; information sharing; privacy protection of customer data.

Memory trick: Security goals CIA (in the grid: Availability and Integrity first). FDI (false data injection) = "a = Hc fools the detector".

B3 Reactive power and voltage control: why the grid needs reactive power, control methods, AVR, SVC, improving Pmax Very likely · 100%Easy

Past-paper questions · Must study

  • 2023 Q5(b) [13] How can the maximum power output (Pmax) of a generator be effectively improved? What are the primary functions of a thyristor-based SVC (static var compensator) in power system? Explain with diagram.
  • 2023 Q6(c) [15] What are the primary methods and devices used to control reactive power in power systems? How does the AVR (automatic voltage regulator) maintain voltage stability in smart grid? (loop part in B2)
  • 2022 Q6(d) [7] Why does the grid need reactive power? Discuss.
  • 2020 Q4(c) [8] What is the necessity of reactive power control in grid? Write the different methods of reactive power control.
★ REMEMBER IT
  • Reactive power (Q) holds up voltage. Too little Q → low voltage, possible voltage collapse. Q sources: generators (AVR), shunt capacitors, synchronous condensers, SVC (static var compensator), STATCOM (static synchronous compensator), tap-changing transformers.
  • Pmax = EV/X: raise E (stronger excitation), raise V (voltage support), or lower X (parallel lines, series capacitors).
Before you start: active and reactive power in plain words

Active power P (watts) does useful work. Reactive power Q (var) does no net work but is needed to build the magnetic fields in motors, transformers and long lines; it also controls voltage. Rule of thumb: P controls frequency and angle, Q controls voltage.

Power through a line: P = (E V / X) sin δ, where E, V are the voltages at the ends, X the line reactance and δ the angle between them. The largest possible value (at δ = 90°) is Pmax = E V / X.

Why the grid needs reactive power (2022 6d, 2020 4c)
  • Inductive loads (induction motors, transformers, fluorescent ballasts, fans, pumps, compressors) need Q for their magnetising fields; without it they cannot work.
  • Lines and transformers absorb Q (I2X); Q must be supplied to keep voltages within limits (±5-10 %). Lack of Q causes low voltage and, in the worst case, voltage collapse (B6).
  • Reactive power supports power transfer: Pmax = EV/X falls when voltages drop.
  • Controlling Q reduces line current, so reduces I2R losses and frees capacity; improves power factor (and avoids pf penalties).
  • Inverter-based renewables must supply/absorb Q to avoid voltage rise/fall on feeders.
Methods and devices to control reactive power (2023 6c, 2020 4c)
Device / methodHow it controls Q and voltage
Generator excitation with AVR (automatic voltage regulator)Over-excited generator supplies Q, under-excited absorbs Q; the AVR holds terminal voltage
Shunt capacitors (fixed or switched)Supply Q at load points, raise voltage, improve pf; cheap
Shunt reactorsAbsorb Q on long lightly-loaded lines / cables (Ferranti effect) to limit over-voltage
Series capacitorsCancel part of line reactance X: more power transfer, better voltage
Synchronous condensersSynchronous motor running without load; continuously variable Q supply/absorption, adds inertia
Tap-changing transformers (OLTC) and regulating transformersAdjust turns ratio to correct voltage (redistribute Q)
SVC (static var compensator)Thyristor-controlled reactor + thyristor-switched capacitor: fast continuous Q control
STATCOM and other FACTS (UPFC, TCSC (thyristor-controlled series capacitor))Voltage-source converter injects controllable Q; faster and better at low voltage than SVC
Inverter-based DG (distributed generation) / storageSmart inverters provide Volt/VAR support (Q droop) on distribution feeders
Load-side: pf correction, demand response, load sheddingReduce Q demand in emergencies
How the AVR maintains voltage stability (2023 6c)

The AVR measures the generator terminal voltage Vt through a sensor (potential transformer + rectifier and filter), compares it with the reference Vref; the error is amplified (amplifier) and drives the exciter, which changes the field current of the generator. If Vt falls (heavy load or reactive demand), the error increases the field current → internal emf E rises → generator supplies more Q → Vt returns to the set value. If Vt rises, excitation is reduced. With fast static exciters and a power system stabiliser (PSS) to damp oscillations, the AVR keeps voltages steady, maintains reactive reserves and improves both voltage and transient stability. In the smart grid, AVR set-points can be coordinated with SVCs, OLTCs and DG inverters by Volt/VAR optimisation.

Improving Pmax of a generator (2023 5b)

Pmax = E V / X

  1. Increase E: higher excitation (fast-acting exciters and AVR, high ceiling voltage).
  2. Increase V: hold the system voltage up with reactive support (SVC, STATCOM, capacitors, synchronous condensers).
  3. Reduce X (most effective): parallel (double-circuit) lines, bundled conductors, series capacitor compensation (TCSC), lower-reactance transformers and generators, higher transmission voltage.
  4. Use FACTS (flexible AC transmission systems)/HVDC to control flows; also fast fault clearing and auto-reclosing to keep the post-fault Pmax high.
Thyristor-based SVC: functions with diagram (2023 5b)

An SVC is a shunt-connected FACTS device made of a thyristor-controlled reactor (TCR) - a reactor in series with back-to-back thyristors whose firing angle (90°-180°) varies the effective inductance continuously - and thyristor-switched capacitors (TSC) switched in steps, plus fixed capacitors/harmonic filters, connected via a step-down transformer. A controller measures the bus voltage and sets the firing angles so the SVC behaves like a variable susceptance, from capacitive (supplying Q) to inductive (absorbing Q).

Functions: fast dynamic voltage control at the bus; reactive power compensation; improving transient stability and increasing power transfer (Pmax); damping power oscillations; reducing voltage flicker (arc furnaces); balancing unbalanced loads; preventing voltage collapse.

Memory trick: P ↔ frequency, Q ↔ voltage. Pmax = EV/X: raise E, raise V, cut X. SVC = TCR (absorbs) + TSC (supplies).

B11 Barriers and solutions, standards and research areas, the simplest and the most complex thing about the smart grid Very likely · 100%Easy

Past-paper questions · Must study

  • 2023 Q8(a) [13] What are the primary barriers to the development of smart grids, and what solutions can be implemented to overcome these obstacles? Discuss.
  • 2022 Q8(c) [8] Why are smart grid standards necessary? What would be the suitable areas of research in smart grid?
  • 2020 Q4(a) [12] What are the simplest thing and the complex thing about the smart grid? (voltage stability part in B6)
★ REMEMBER IT
  • Barriers: high cost, unclear regulation, interoperability/standards, cyber security and privacy, skills shortage, customer acceptance. Solutions: pilot projects, standards, incentives, training, public awareness.
Before you start: why smart grids are slow to come

The idea is simple, but turning a century-old grid into a smart one costs a lot, needs new rules, new skills and common standards, and must be safe against hackers. This topic lists those barriers, their solutions, the role of standards and the open research areas.

The simplest and the most complex thing about the smart grid (2020 4a)

Simplest: the concept itself - add sensing, two-way communication and computer control to the existing power grid so that it can monitor itself and respond automatically ("an internet for electricity"). Many pieces (smart meters, SCADA (supervisory control and data acquisition), automation) already exist and can be added step by step.

Most complex: making it all work together - integrating millions of heterogeneous devices, variable renewables, storage and EVs, markets and active customers in real time, with interoperability, stability, data management and cyber security, under uncertain regulation and economics. The power system is the largest machine ever built; changing it while it runs is a huge systems-engineering challenge.

Primary barriers and solutions (2023 8a)
BarrierSolution
High capital cost, uncertain payback, utilities' limited financePhased deployment starting with high-benefit projects (prepaid/smart meters, loss reduction); cost-benefit studies; government funds, green bonds, development banks (ADB, World Bank), public-private partnerships
Regulatory and policy barriers: tariffs that reward selling more kWh, no time-of-use pricing, unclear cost recoverySmart grid roadmap and policy; regulator (BERC) to allow cost recovery, performance-based regulation, dynamic tariffs, net metering
Lack of standards and interoperability; legacy equipmentAdopt international standards (IEC 61850, CIM (common information model), IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 2030); open architecture; pilot testing
Cyber security and privacy concernsSecurity by design, standards (NISTIR 7628, IEC (International Electrotechnical Commission) 62351), data protection law, monitoring
Technical complexity: integrating renewables, stability, communication coverageResearch, pilots and demonstration projects; storage; advanced control and AI
Skills shortageEducation and training programmes, university-industry collaboration
Consumer acceptance: privacy fears, distrust of new meters and bills, low awarenessAwareness campaigns, transparent billing, apps, incentives, protecting data
Institutional inertia, many stakeholders with different interestsStrong leadership, stakeholder coordination, clear roles
Why smart grid standards are necessary (2022 8c)
  • Interoperability: devices and systems from different vendors work together (plug and play).
  • Reduce cost and risk: competition among vendors, avoid lock-in and stranded assets, economies of scale.
  • Security and safety: common cyber security and electrical safety requirements.
  • Reliability and quality: performance requirements (e.g. PMU (phasor measurement unit) accuracy IEEE C37.118, DG (distributed generation) interconnection IEEE 1547, PQ IEEE 519).
  • Scalability and future-proofing: allow upgrades and new applications.
  • Facilitate regulation, certification, international trade and knowledge sharing.
Suitable areas of research in smart grid (2022 8c)
  • Renewable and load forecasting; integration of high renewable shares (grid-forming inverters, synthetic inertia).
  • Energy storage technologies and their optimal operation; EVs and V2G (vehicle-to-grid).
  • Microgrids, nanogrids, virtual power plants, peer-to-peer energy trading (blockchain).
  • Wide-area monitoring, protection and control with PMUs; real-time state estimation.
  • Cyber security (false data injection detection), privacy-preserving analytics.
  • AI and big data for operation, predictive maintenance and theft detection; DSOPF (dynamic stochastic optimal power flow) and optimisation under uncertainty.
  • Demand response and customer behaviour; dynamic pricing and market design.
  • Communication networks (5G, IoT (Internet of Things)) for the grid; interoperability standards.
  • Power quality with power electronics; adaptive protection in active networks; resilience to climate disasters.

Memory trick: Barriers = "Cost, Rules, Standards, Security, Skills, Society".

B10 Renewables and the smart grid: integration challenges, education and training, V2G, sustainable energy options, efficiency and DG control Very likely · 83%Easy

Past-paper questions · Must study

  • 2023 Q7(a) [12] What are some current research challenges in integrating renewable energy sources into the smart grid infrastructure? How does education and training contribute to the successful implementation of smart grid?
  • 2023 Q6(b) [8] Write a short note on vehicle-to-grid (V2G) technology.
  • 2022 Q8(a) [8] How does a smart grid improve efficiency? What are the benefits of distributed generation control in smart grid?
  • 2022 Q8(b) [7] Give an overview of sustainable energy options for the smart grid.
★ REMEMBER IT
  • V2G (vehicle-to-grid): parked EVs plugged in can send stored energy back to the grid at peak times and charge at night: a huge distributed battery for frequency and peak support.
Before you start: renewables, EVs and efficiency

Solar and wind are clean but variable (clouds, wind gusts) and uncertain; they connect through inverters (no spinning mass, so less inertia) and are spread over many small sites. The smart grid gives the tools to integrate them: forecasting, storage, flexible demand and fast control.

An electric vehicle is a big battery on wheels that is parked about 95 % of the time. V2G (vehicle-to-grid) (vehicle-to-grid) lets it give power back to the grid when needed.

Research challenges in integrating renewables (2023 7a)
  1. Variability and forecasting: accurate short-term solar/wind forecasts; probabilistic planning and operation.
  2. Low inertia and stability: frequency and voltage stability with high inverter share; grid-forming inverters, synthetic inertia, fast frequency response.
  3. Energy storage: low-cost, long-life storage, optimal sizing and control.
  4. Distribution impacts: voltage rise, reverse power flow, hosting capacity, protection coordination and islanding detection.
  5. Power quality: harmonics and flicker from inverters.
  6. Control and optimisation: coordinated control of millions of DERs, microgrids, virtual power plants, demand response.
  7. Market and regulatory design: pricing flexibility and ancillary services, net metering.
  8. Communication, data and cyber security for distributed resources; interoperability standards.

Role of education and training: smart grids need engineers and technicians skilled in power systems, power electronics, ICT (information and communication technology), data science and cyber security together. Education and training (university courses, vocational programmes, utility staff training, simulators, certification) build this workforce; they help operators use new tools (DMS, WAMS (wide area monitoring system)), reduce errors, support research and innovation, and inform consumers so they participate in demand response, rooftop PV and EVs. Without trained people, smart grid investments fail.

Vehicle-to-grid (V2G) technology (2023 6b)

V2G is a system in which plug-in electric vehicles communicate with the grid and, through a bidirectional charger, can both draw power (G2V, grid-to-vehicle) and return stored energy to the grid (V2G), controlled by the utility or an aggregator according to price and grid needs.

  • Services: peak shaving (discharge at evening peak), valley filling (charge at night), frequency regulation and spinning reserve (fast response), voltage support, storing surplus solar/wind, emergency backup (vehicle-to-home, V2H (vehicle-to-home)).
  • Benefits: cheaper grid operation, better renewable integration, extra income for EV owners, less need for peaking plants.
  • Challenges: battery degradation from extra cycling, cost of bidirectional chargers, communication and standards (ISO 15118), aggregation of many small vehicles, owner availability and willingness, cyber security.
How a smart grid improves efficiency; benefits of DG (distributed generation) control (2022 8a)
  • Loss reduction: Volt/VAR optimisation, conservation voltage reduction, network reconfiguration, power factor correction, DG close to loads.
  • Peak reduction and load-factor improvement by DSM (demand side management) and storage: fewer inefficient peaking plants, better use of assets.
  • Better asset utilisation: dynamic line rating, condition-based maintenance, fewer outages.
  • Informed consumers: real-time data and time-of-use prices reduce waste (typically 5-15 % savings).
  • Integration of efficient and clean generation (CHP, renewables).

Benefits of distributed generation control: keeps feeder voltages within limits (reactive power control of inverters); prevents reverse-flow overloads; enables DG to provide ancillary services (frequency response, reserves); coordinated dispatch minimises losses and cost; supports islanding and microgrid operation for reliability; increases DG hosting capacity; smooths renewable output with storage; allows virtual power plants to take part in markets.

Sustainable energy options for the smart grid (2022 8b)
OptionRole
Solar PV (rooftop, solar parks), solar thermalLargest growth in Bangladesh; distributed generation with smart inverters
Wind (onshore, offshore)Bulk renewable energy; needs forecasting and balancing
Hydro and pumped hydroFlexible renewable generation and large-scale storage (Kaptai)
Biomass, biogas, waste-to-energyDispatchable renewable DG, rural mini-grids
Geothermal, tidal/waveLocation-specific renewables
Fuel cells and green hydrogenClean DG, long-term storage, CHP (combined heat and power)
Energy storage (batteries, flywheels, supercapacitors)Firm up renewables, ancillary services
Electric vehicles and V2GFlexible load and mobile storage
Energy efficiency, CHP, demand responseThe cheapest "resource": reduce demand and losses
Nuclear (low carbon)Base-load low-carbon supply (Rooppur)

Memory trick: Renewable challenges = "Variable, Uncertain, Low-inertia, Distributed". V2G = charge at night, give back at peak, regulate frequency.

B7 Power quality: issues in a smart grid, importance of power-quality management and audit Very likely · 83%Easy

Past-paper questions · Must study

  • 2023 Q5(c) [7] Why is power quality management in smart grid so important?
  • 2022 Q5(b) [8] What are the power quality issues with smart grid? What is the importance of power quality audit in smart grid? Discuss.
★ REMEMBER IT
  • Power quality problems: sags/swells, harmonics, flicker, transients, interruptions, unbalance, frequency deviation. Smart grids have more of them because of inverters (harmonics) and variable renewables (fluctuations).
Before you start: clean power

Ideal electricity is a perfect 50 Hz sine wave at exactly rated voltage, never interrupted. Anything that distorts or disturbs this is a power quality (PQ) problem. Computers, drives, PLCs and medical equipment are very sensitive to it, and the smart grid adds many power-electronic sources (inverters) that can create it.

Power quality issues in a smart grid (2022 5b)
IssueMeaningTypical cause
Voltage sag (dip)Short drop to 10-90 % for 0.5 cycle-1 minFaults, motor starting
SwellShort rise above 110 %Single-line faults, load switching off, DG (distributed generation)
InterruptionVoltage < 10 % (momentary to sustained)Faults, breaker operation
Transients / surgesVery fast spikesLightning, capacitor switching
HarmonicsWaveform distortion at multiples of 50 Hz (THD)Inverters, VFDs, LEDs, SMPS (switched-mode power supply), EV chargers
Flicker / voltage fluctuationRepeated small variations visible in lampsArc furnaces, wind/PV output variation
UnbalanceUnequal three-phase voltagesSingle-phase loads and rooftop PV
Frequency deviationDeparture from 50 HzGeneration-load imbalance, low inertia
DC offset, notching, noise
Importance of power quality management in the smart grid (2023 5c)
  • Sensitive digital loads (computers, PLCs, medical, telecom, data centres) malfunction or fail; industrial process interruptions cost a lot.
  • Harmonics cause overheating of transformers, cables and motors, extra losses, capacitor failure, nuisance tripping and metering errors.
  • High penetration of inverter-based renewables, EV chargers and LEDs increases harmonics, voltage rise and flicker - must be managed.
  • Smart grid communication and sensing equipment itself needs clean power.
  • Better PQ = higher efficiency, longer equipment life, customer satisfaction and compliance with standards (IEEE 519, IEC (International Electrotechnical Commission) 61000, EN 50160).
  • Smart meters and PMUs make continuous PQ monitoring possible, and FACTS (flexible AC transmission systems)/custom power devices (DVR, STATCOM (static synchronous compensator), active filters, UPS (uninterruptible power supply)) fix problems.
Importance of power quality audit (2022 5b)

A PQ audit is a systematic measurement and analysis of voltage, current, harmonics, sags, flicker, pf and unbalance at a site (with PQ analysers over a period), comparing with standards, finding sources and recommending solutions.

  1. Identifies PQ problems and their sources before equipment is damaged.
  2. Quantifies losses (harmonic and reactive) and energy-saving potential; pf correction.
  3. Guides the right mitigation: filters, UPS, DVR (dynamic voltage restorer), isolation transformers, wiring/grounding fixes.
  4. Verifies compliance with grid codes and standards (important for DG/PV connection).
  5. Gives a baseline for planning and for contracts between utility and customer.
  6. Improves reliability and reduces downtime and maintenance costs.

Memory trick: PQ problems = "Sag, Swell, Stop (interruption), Spike, Harmonics, Flicker, Unbalance".

B2 Frequency control: why grid frequency matters, turbine speed governing system, load frequency control loop, AGC Very likely · 100%Medium

Past-paper questions · Must study

  • 2023 Q6(c) [15] Draw and discuss the simple feedback loop block diagram of generator and load. What are the primary methods and devices used to control reactive power in power systems? And how does the AVR (automatic voltage regulator) maintain the voltage stability in smart grid? (reactive power part in B3)
  • 2022 Q5(c) [12] Why is power grid frequency important? How does the turbine speed governing system work? Explain with schematic diagram.
  • 2022 Q5(d) [9] What is Automatic Generation Control (AGC) in power system? "AGC (automatic generation control) is essential in smart grid" - justify.
  • 2020 Q6(b) [12] What is false data injection attack in the smart grid? "Automatic Generation Control (AGC) is essential for power system" - justify. (attack part in B9)
UNDERSTAND Read this to understand; you do not need to write it

Frequency shows the balance of generation and load in real time. More load than generation → generators slow down → frequency falls. The governor (primary control) senses speed and opens the steam/water valve within seconds, but leaves a small steady error set by the droop R. AGC (automatic generation control, secondary control) then slowly resets the governor set-points so frequency returns exactly to 50 Hz and tie-line flows to schedule.

Interactive calculator (needs JavaScript; open the HTML version).

Before you start: why frequency tells you the balance

All generators in a grid spin in step (synchronously). Frequency (50 Hz in Bangladesh) is proportional to their speed. If load suddenly rises and generation does not, the extra energy is taken from the spinning rotors, they slow down and frequency falls. If generation exceeds load, frequency rises. So frequency is the live indicator of the generation-load balance.

Control happens in layers: inertia (instant), primary control by each machine's speed governor (seconds; frequency settles a little below 50 Hz), secondary control = AGC (minutes; brings frequency exactly back to 50 Hz), then tertiary/economic dispatch.

Why grid frequency is important (2022 5c)
  • It shows the real-power balance; a big deviation means a generation-load mismatch that can lead to under-frequency load shedding or a blackout.
  • Motors' speed and many industrial processes depend on frequency; clocks and timing devices use it.
  • Generators and steam turbine blades can be damaged by operation away from rated frequency (blade resonance); transformers and motors overheat at low frequency (higher flux).
  • Protection relays trip units outside the allowed band (e.g. 49.0-51.0 Hz), which can cascade.
  • Interconnected areas must hold scheduled frequency to keep tie-line flows correct.
Turbine speed governing system (2022 5c)
  1. Speed governor (fly-ball or electronic sensor) driven from the turbine shaft senses speed. When speed falls, the fly-balls move in and point B of the linkage moves.
  2. Linkage mechanism converts the fly-ball movement into a displacement of the pilot valve (point C); it also gives feedback from the main piston so the valve settles at a new position (this gives the droop R).
  3. Speed changer (load reference set-point, motor-driven): moved manually or by AGC to change the output at a given frequency.
  4. Hydraulic amplifier: the small pilot-valve movement admits high-pressure oil to the main piston, which produces the large force needed to move the steam valve (point D).
  5. Steam (or water) control valve opens more, turbine power rises, generator speed and frequency recover; the final frequency is slightly lower than before (steady-state error = R × ΔP).

Steady-state: Δf = −R ΔPL / (1 + DR)   (R = droop, Hz/MW or pu; 5 % droop typical)

Simple feedback loop block diagram of generator and load (2023 6c)

The loop: a change in reference ΔPref minus the speed feedback Δω/R drives the governor (time constant Tg ≈ 0.2 s), which moves the valve ΔPV; the turbine (Tt ≈ 0.5 s) changes mechanical power ΔPm; ΔPm − ΔPL (load change) acts on the generator-load block 1/(2Hs + D) (H = inertia constant, D = load damping) giving the speed/frequency deviation Δω, which is fed back through the droop 1/R. This primary loop limits the frequency drop; a steady error remains unless AGC adds an integral loop that changes ΔPref.

Automatic generation control (AGC) and why it is essential in the smart grid (2022 5d, 2020 6b)

AGC is the secondary control system that automatically adjusts the set-points (speed changers) of selected generators to (1) restore system frequency to its scheduled value (50 Hz) after primary control, (2) keep tie-line power flows between control areas at their scheduled values, and (3) share load among generators economically. It works on the area control error: ACE (area control error) = ΔPtie + BΔf (B = frequency bias); an integral controller drives ACE to zero every few seconds.

"AGC is essential" - justification:

  1. Primary control alone leaves a permanent frequency error; only AGC removes it.
  2. Keeps interchange with neighbours at contract values (important for Bangladesh-India links).
  3. Renewables (solar, wind) cause fast, random power fluctuations and reduce inertia; AGC continuously balances them, helped by fast storage and demand response in the smart grid.
  4. Economic: re-allocates load to the cheapest units (with economic dispatch).
  5. Prevents under-frequency load shedding and cascading blackouts, so improves reliability.
  6. Smart grid AGC uses PMU (phasor measurement unit) data, storage, EVs (V2G) and responsive loads as regulation resources.

Memory trick: Frequency = balance meter. Layers: inertia (instant) → governor/droop (seconds) → AGC/integral of ACE (minutes) → dispatch. Governor chain: "Fly-balls, Linkage, Hydraulic amplifier, Valve".

B6 Voltage stability: why instability occurs, preventive control, assessment techniques (P-V, Q-V, VIPI, indices) Very likely · 100%Medium

Past-paper questions · Must study

  • 2023 Q8(c) [12] Mention the names of different voltage stability assessment techniques. Describe one of them.
  • 2022 Q7(a) [8] Why does voltage instability occur in power grid? Discuss the voltage instability preventive control scheme for the power grid.
  • 2020 Q4(a) [12] What are the simplest thing and the complex thing about the smart grid? Write about the major reasons for voltage stability problems in power system. (first part in B11)
  • 2020 Q5(b) [10] Classify the techniques of voltage stability assessment. Describe the VIPI (voltage instability proximity index) method for voltage stability assessment.
UNDERSTAND Read this to understand; you do not need to write it

Voltage instability happens when the network cannot deliver the reactive power the loads need: heavy loading, long lines, generators hitting their Q limits, or a line trip. Voltage then sags, motor loads draw more current, voltage sags more, until it collapses.

P-V curve ("nose curve"): as load P rises, voltage falls slowly then suddenly; the tip of the nose is the maximum loadability, and the distance from today's load to the nose is the stability margin.

Interactive graph (needs JavaScript; open the HTML version).

Before you start: voltage collapse

As you draw more and more power through a line, the receiving-end voltage falls slowly at first, then faster, until a point where drawing more makes the voltage crash - the tip of the P-V "nose" curve. Beyond that tip no steady operating point exists: voltage collapse (blackout).

The root cause is shortage of reactive power at the load end (Q controls voltage).

Why voltage instability occurs (2022 7a, 2020 4a)

Voltage instability is the inability of a power system to maintain acceptable voltages at all buses after a disturbance or load increase; voltages fall progressively and uncontrollably. Major reasons:

  1. Heavy loading and long transmission distances (large reactance → large reactive losses I2X).
  2. Shortage of reactive power: generators reaching field-current (Q) limits, capacitor banks whose output falls with V2.
  3. Outage of lines or generators (contingencies) that weaken the network.
  4. On-load tap changers restoring load-side voltage, which increases current and reactive demand on the weak transmission system.
  5. Load characteristics: constant-power loads, induction motors that stall at low voltage and draw high reactive current, air-conditioners.
  6. Poor coordination of controls and protection; low power factor loads; high penetration of inverter-based DG (distributed generation) without voltage support.
Voltage instability preventive control scheme (2022 7a)
  • Keep adequate reactive power reserves on generators, SVCs and STATCOMs; switch in shunt capacitors, switch out reactors.
  • Raise generator voltage set-points (AVR) and coordinate secondary voltage control.
  • Block or reverse OLTC (on-load tap changer) action during emergencies.
  • Re-dispatch generation closer to load centres; reduce transfers on weak corridors.
  • Demand response and under-voltage load shedding as the last resort.
  • On-line voltage stability assessment with PMUs, stability margins (distance to the nose), alarms and wide-area special protection schemes.
Voltage stability assessment techniques (2023 8c, 2020 5b)
ClassTechniques
Static (steady-state) methodsP-V curve analysis; Q-V curve analysis (reactive margin); continuation power flow (CPF) to trace the nose; modal (eigenvalue) analysis of the reduced Jacobian; singular value decomposition; minimum singular value of Jacobian
Voltage stability indicesL-index (Kessel-Glavitsch), line indices (Lmn, FVSI, LQP), VIPI (voltage instability proximity index), tangent vector index, sensitivity dV/dQ
Dynamic methodsTime-domain simulation including OLTCs, loads and limiters; small-signal analysis
Measurement-based / intelligent methodsThevenin equivalent from PMU (phasor measurement unit) data (impedance matching), ANN (artificial neural network), decision trees, expert systems
Described method: VIPI (2020 5b)

The voltage instability proximity index (VIPI) (Tamura) uses the fact that a load-flow problem has two solutions for every loading below the critical point: the normal high-voltage solution and an abnormal low-voltage solution. As the load increases these two solutions move towards each other and coincide at the critical (nose) point.

  1. Solve the load flow for the present loading and obtain the high-voltage solution vector x1 and the low-voltage (multiple) solution x2.
  2. Form two vectors in the space of the specified quantities: from the origin to the specified load vector ys, and to the "singular" vector y(xc) at the midpoint xc = (x1 + x2)/2.
  3. VIPI = the angle θ between these vectors: cosθ = (ys·y(xc)) / (|ys||y(xc)|).
  4. Far from collapse the solutions are far apart and θ is large; as loading approaches the critical point θ → 0.
  5. So VIPI gives a scalar measure of how close the system is to voltage collapse; operators act (preventive control) when it falls below a threshold.

Advantages: one number for the whole system, uses load-flow results; disadvantage: finding the low-voltage solution needs extra computation. (Alternatively describe the P-V curve method: increase load step by step, run load flow, plot V against P; the distance from the operating point to the nose is the MW margin.)

Memory trick: Voltage collapse = "not enough Q at the end of a long, heavy line". Methods: "PV, QV, CPF (continuation power flow), Modal, Indices (L, VIPI), Dynamic, PMU/AI".

B1 Buses and bus types, infinite bus, bus admittance matrix Ybus and proof of Ibus = YbusVbus Very likely · 83%Medium

Past-paper questions · Must study

  • 2023 Q5(a) [15] What are the bus and infinite bus in power system? Describe a method to derive the bus admittance matrix in smart power system and prove that Ibus = YbusVbus.
  • 2022 Q5(a) [6] How many buses are there in the power system? What is the significance of different types of buses in the power system?
LEARN IT FROM ZERO
Bus admittance matrix, from zero

Write Kirchhoff's current law at every bus: the current injected at bus i equals the sum of currents leaving through all the lines connected to it. With line admittance yij = 1/zij, current from i to j is yij(Vi − Vj). Collect the terms of each V and you get I = YbusV.

The rules fall out automatically: diagonal Yii = sum of every admittance connected to bus i (including shunt to ground); off-diagonal Yij = −yij (minus the line between i and j, zero if no line). Ybus is symmetric and mostly zeros (sparse).

Interactive calculator (needs JavaScript; open the HTML version).

Before you start: buses and the admittance matrix

A bus is just a junction (node) in the power network where generators, loads and lines meet - like a junction in a pipe network.

Admittance y = 1/z (z = impedance, in ohms or per unit); it says how easily current flows. Kirchhoff's current law (KCL) at each bus says: current injected into the bus = sum of currents leaving through the lines. Write KCL (Kirchhoff's current law) for every bus and you get a matrix equation I = Y V. Ybus is the "wiring map" of the network in numbers.

Per unit (pu) = value divided by a base value, so 1.0 pu means rated.

Bus, types of buses and their significance (2023 5a, 2022 5a)

A bus is a node in the power system at which one or more lines, generators or loads are connected. For load flow, each bus has four quantities: real power P, reactive power Q, voltage magnitude |V| and angle δ; two are specified and two are calculated. So there are three types of buses:

Bus typeSpecifiedUnknownSignificance
Slack (swing / reference) bus - only one|V| and δ (usually 1.0∠0°)P, QProvides the angle reference; supplies the system losses and balances generation and load, which are unknown before the solution
PV (generator / voltage-controlled) busP and |V|Q, δGenerators (and SVCs) whose excitation holds the voltage; Q must stay within limits (if a limit is hit, it becomes a PQ bus)
PQ (load) bus - most busesP and Q|V|, δLoad buses (and buses with fixed-output DG (distributed generation)); their voltages are what the study checks

Classification is needed because the load-flow equations can be solved only when exactly two quantities per bus are known. In smart grids, DG with voltage control may be PV buses, DG at fixed power PQ buses, and droop-controlled units special buses.

Infinite bus (2023 5a)

An infinite bus is an idealised bus whose voltage magnitude and frequency remain constant regardless of how much power is injected or drawn - it has zero internal impedance and infinite inertia. A single generator connected to a very large grid sees the grid as an infinite bus; it is used in stability studies (B4) and in machine analysis (B5).

Deriving Ybus and proving Ibus = YbusVbus (2023 5a)

Method: represent each line by its series admittance yij = 1/zij and shunt admittances yi0 to ground; replace generators and loads by current injections Ii (positive into the bus). Apply KCL at each bus.

Step (write this)Why / what it means
Bus 1: I1 = y10V1 + y12(V1 − V2) + y13(V1 − V3)Injected current = current to ground + currents leaving through each line (KCL). Line current = admittance × voltage difference.
I1 = (y10 + y12 + y13)V1 − y12V2 − y13V3Collect the terms of each voltage.
Bus 2: I2 = −y12V1 + (y20 + y12 + y23)V2 − y23V3Same for bus 2.
Bus 3: I3 = −y13V1 − y23V2 + (y30 + y13 + y23)V3Same for bus 3 (a load bus has a negative injection).
Define Yii = yi0 + Σj yij (self/driving-point admittance) and Yij = −yij (mutual/transfer admittance)Diagonal = sum of all admittances connected to the bus; off-diagonal = negative of the admittance joining the two buses (0 if not connected).
Ii = Σj=1n YijVj,   i = 1 ... nEvery bus equation has this same form.
[I1; I2; I3] = [Y11 Y12 Y13; Y21 Y22 Y23; Y31 Y32 Y33][V1; V2; V3] ⇒ Ibus = YbusVbusWrite the n equations in matrix form: proved.

Properties of Ybus: square (n × n), symmetric (Yij = Yji without phase shifters), complex, highly sparse (most buses are not directly connected), diagonally dominant; built easily by inspection; its inverse is Zbus. It is the basis of Gauss-Seidel and Newton-Raphson load flow (A9) and of state estimation in the smart grid.

Memory trick: "Diagonal = sum of all, off-diagonal = minus the link". Bus types: Slack (Vδ), PV, PQ - the two letters are what you KNOW.

B4 Rotor angle stability: steady-state vs transient, swing equation, small-disturbance solution ωn = √(πf0Ps/H), equal area criterion Very likely · 83%Hard

Past-paper questions · Must study

  • 2023 Q6(a) [12] In power system transient stability analysis, what principle does the equal area criterion (EAC) assess? Describe with necessary schematic diagram.
  • 2022 Q6(a) [8] Distinguish between transient and steady-state stability and discuss the need for performing stability analyses of power system.
  • 2022 Q6(b) [6] Elucidate the importance and role of the swing equation in power system stability analysis.
  • 2022 Q6(c) [14] Discuss the possible solutions of the disturbed motion of a synchronous generator connected to an infinite bus, when subjected to a small disturbance represented by Δδ, and prove that ωn = √(πf0Ps/H).
LEARN IT FROM ZERO
Rotor angle stability, from zero

A generator sends power P = (EV/X) sin δ to the grid, where δ is the angle between its internal voltage and the grid voltage. The turbine pushes with Pm; the grid pulls back with Pe. Where the two are equal (δ0), the rotor sits steady.

After a fault Pe drops, so Pm > Pe and the rotor speeds up: δ grows (area A1, acceleration). When the fault is cleared Pe jumps above Pm and the rotor slows down (area A2, deceleration). Equal area criterion: it is stable if the decelerating area available above Pm can be at least as large as the accelerating area. Clear the fault too late and A1 becomes too big.

For a small push, the swing equation (H/πf0) d²Δδ/dt² + PsΔδ = 0 is a spring-mass equation, so δ oscillates at ωn = √(πf0Ps/H), with Ps = Pmax cos δ0 (synchronising power coefficient). Stable only if Ps > 0, i.e. δ0 < 90°.

Interactive graph (needs JavaScript; open the HTML version).

Interactive calculator (needs JavaScript; open the HTML version).

Before you start: the swinging rotor

A synchronous generator connected to the grid is like a car towing a trailer with an elastic rope: the rotor angle δ is the stretch of the rope. Mechanical input power Pm pushes the rotor forward; electrical output Pe = Pmax sin δ pulls it back. If Pm = Pe, δ is steady.

After a disturbance, the rotor swings (oscillates) around a new angle. Stable = the swings die down; unstable = δ keeps growing and the machine loses synchronism (pole-slipping).

H = inertia constant (seconds) = stored kinetic energy / machine rating; f0 = 50 Hz.

Transient vs steady-state stability and the need for stability analysis (2022 6a)
Steady-state (small-signal) stabilityTransient stability
Ability to stay in synchronism after small, gradual disturbances (slow load changes)Ability to stay in synchronism after a large, sudden disturbance (fault, loss of a line or generator, big load switching)
Equations can be linearised around the operating pointNon-linear equations; time-domain simulation or equal area criterion
Limit: steady-state stability limit (Pmax = EV/X at δ = 90°)Limit: transient stability limit (lower than steady-state limit); critical clearing time
Depends on operating point, AVR (automatic voltage regulator), PSS (power system stabiliser)Depends on fault type, location, clearing time, inertia, post-fault network

Need: to find maximum safe power transfers and operating limits; to set protection and critical fault clearing times; to design controllers (AVR, PSS, governors, FACTS (flexible AC transmission systems)); to plan new lines and generators; to prevent blackouts. In smart grids, inverter-based renewables reduce inertia and change dynamics, so stability analysis is even more important.

Swing equation: importance and role (2022 6b)

(2H/ωs) d2δ/dt2 = Pm − Pe   or   (H/πf0) d2δ/dt2 = Pm − Pmax sinδ   (pu, δ in electrical radians)

It is Newton's second law for the rotor (inertia × angular acceleration = accelerating power). Role: it is the fundamental equation of rotor-angle stability - it describes how δ changes with time after a disturbance; solving it (numerically, step by step) shows whether δ settles (stable) or increases without limit (unstable); it gives the basis for the equal area criterion, small-signal analysis, critical clearing angle and time, and for designing controls and protection.

Solution for a small disturbance and proof of ωn = √(πf0Ps/H) (2022 6c)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
(H/πf0) d2δ/dt2 + Pmax sinδ = PmSwing equation with Pe = Pmax sinδ (machine on an infinite bus).
Let δ = δ0 + Δδ; sin(δ0 + Δδ) ≈ sinδ0 + cosδ0·ΔδSmall disturbance: sinΔδ ≈ Δδ, cosΔδ ≈ 1.
(H/πf0) d2Δδ/dt2 + Pmaxcosδ0·Δδ = 0Initial balance Pm = Pmax sinδ0 cancels; d2δ0/dt2 = 0.
Ps = dPe/dδ |δ0 = Pmax cosδ0Synchronising power coefficient = slope of the power-angle curve.
(H/πf0) d2Δδ/dt2 + PsΔδ = 0A linear 2nd-order equation, like a mass on a spring.
Characteristic equation: s2 + (πf0Ps/H) = 0 ⇒ s = ± j√(πf0Ps/H)Put Δδ = est.
ωn = √(πf0Ps/H) rad/s; fn = ωn/2πProved: the natural frequency of rotor oscillation.
If Ps > 0 (δ0 < 90°): Δδ(t) = Δδ0 cosωnt → sustained oscillation, stableRoots purely imaginary. With damping D the oscillations decay: Δδ = (Δδ0/√(1−ζ2)) e−ζωnt sin(ωdt + θ).
If Ps < 0 (δ0 > 90°): s = ±√(πf0|Ps|/H), one root positive → Δδ grows exponentially, unstableOperating beyond the peak of the P-δ curve.

Side note: Typical numbers: H = 5 s, f0 = 50 Hz, Ps = 1.5 pu → ωn = √(π × 50 × 1.5 / 5) = 6.86 rad/s, fn ≈ 1.1 Hz: the typical 1-2 Hz local mode of power swings.

Equal area criterion (2023 6a)

The equal area criterion (EAC) is a graphical method to judge the transient stability of a single machine connected to an infinite bus (or two machines) without solving the swing equation in time. It assesses whether the kinetic energy the rotor gains during a disturbance can be given back to the system before the angle passes the unstable point.

  1. Before the fault the machine runs at δ0 where Pm = Pe.
  2. During a fault Pe drops (to zero for a three-phase fault at the terminals) while Pm is constant, so the rotor accelerates: kinetic energy gained = area A1 = ∫(Pm − Pe)dδ from δ0 to the clearing angle δc.
  3. After clearing, Pe > Pm, the rotor decelerates; it gives back energy = area A2 = ∫(Pe − Pm)dδ from δc to δmax.
  4. The rotor stops swinging forward when A2 = A1. The system is stable if an A2 equal to A1 is available before δ reaches the unstable point δmax = 180° − δ0.
  5. The critical clearing angle δcr makes A1 = maximum available A2; for Pe = 0 during the fault: cosδcr = (π − 2δ0) sinδ0 − cosδ0; critical clearing time tcr = √[4H(δcr − δ0)/(ωsPm)].

Memory trick: Swing equation = "Inertia × acceleration = Pm − Pe". Small signal: ωn = √(πf0Ps/H) - "pi f P over H, root it". EAC (equal area criterion): "energy gained (A1) must be paid back (A2)".

B5 Numerical: voltage behind transient reactance and transient power-angle equation (with and without saliency) Possible · 17%Hard

Past-paper questions · Good to have

  • 2020 Q4(b) [10] A synchronous machine has xd = 1.0, xq = 0.6, x′d = 0.3 pu and negligible armature resistance. It is connected directly to an infinite bus of 1.0 pu and delivers 0.5 pu real power at 0.8 pf lagging. Determine the voltage behind transient reactance and the transient power-angle equation (i) neglecting saliency, (ii) including saliency.
UNDERSTAND Read this to understand; you do not need to write it

A generator in a transient study is a voltage E′ behind its transient reactance x′d. Find E′ by walking from the infinite bus through x′d: E′ = V + jx′dI. Then Pe = (E′V/x′d) sin δ. A salient-pole machine adds a reluctance term (V²/2)(1/xq − 1/x′d) sin 2δ.

Always check: put δ0 back in your equation; it must give the original P (0.5 pu here).

Symbols used here
SymbolName and meaningUnit
xd, xqDirect- and quadrature-axis synchronous reactancepu
x′dTransient direct-axis reactancepu
VInfinite bus voltage (reference, 1∠0°)pu
I, φArmature current and power-factor angle (lagging = negative)pu, deg
E′Voltage behind transient reactancepu
EQFictitious emf on the q-axis (gives the true rotor angle)pu
Idd-axis current componentpu

Interactive calculator (needs JavaScript; open the HTML version).

Before you start: the machine behind a reactance

For transient studies a synchronous machine is drawn as a voltage source E′ behind its transient reactance x′d. We find E′ from the operating point: E′ = V + j x I (phasor KVL (Kirchhoff's voltage law)).

A salient-pole machine (projecting poles, e.g. hydro) has different reactances along the pole axis (d-axis) and between poles (q-axis), so its power-angle curve gets an extra sin 2δ term (reluctance power).

j = √−1 rotates a phasor by 90°. Lagging pf 0.8 means current lags voltage by cos−10.8 = 36.87°.

Numerical (2020 4b)

Data: xd = 1.0, xq = 0.6, x′d = 0.3 pu, V = 1.0∠0° pu (infinite bus), P = 0.5 pu, pf = 0.8 lagging.

Step (write this)Why / what it means
|I| = P/(V·pf) = 0.5/(1 × 0.8) = 0.625 pu; φ = −36.87°Current magnitude from P = VI cosφ; lagging means negative angle.
I = 0.625∠−36.87° = 0.5 − j0.375 puWrite in rectangular form (0.625 × 0.8 = 0.5, 0.625 × 0.6 = 0.375).

(i) Neglecting saliency (x′d behind the bus):

Step (write this)Why / what it means
E′ = V + jx′dI = 1 + j0.3(0.5 − j0.375)KVL from the infinite bus to the internal emf.
= 1 + 0.1125 + j0.15 = 1.1125 + j0.15j × (−j) = +1.
E′ = 1.1226∠7.68° pu|E′| = √(1.11252 + 0.152); δ0 = tan−1(0.15/1.1125).
Pe = (E′V/x′d) sinδ = (1.1226 × 1/0.3) sinδ = 3.742 sinδTransient power-angle equation. Check: 3.742 sin7.68° = 0.50 pu ✓

(ii) Including saliency:

Step (write this)Why / what it means
EQ = V + jxqI = 1 + j0.6(0.5 − j0.375) = 1.225 + j0.3 = 1.2612∠13.76°This fictitious emf lies on the q-axis, so it gives the true rotor angle δ0 = 13.76°.
Id = |I| sin(δ0 + |φ|) = 0.625 sin(13.76° + 36.87°) = 0.625 × 0.7731 = 0.4832 pud-axis component of the current (angle between I and the q-axis is δ0 + |φ|).
E′q = |EQ| − (xq − x′d)Id = 1.2612 − (0.6 − 0.3)(0.4832)Voltage behind transient reactance on the q-axis.
E′q = 1.1162 pu (at δ0 = 13.76°)
Pe = (E′qV/x′d) sinδ + (V2/2)(1/xq − 1/x′d) sin2δTransient power-angle equation of a salient-pole machine (x′q = xq).
= (1.1162/0.3) sinδ + 0.5(1/0.6 − 1/0.3) sin2δSubstitute.
Pe = 3.721 sinδ − 0.833 sin2δCheck at 13.76°: 3.721(0.2378) − 0.833(0.4621) = 0.885 − 0.385 = 0.50 pu ✓

Side note: Saliency shifts the rotor angle (13.76° vs 7.68°) and adds a negative reluctance term during the transient (because x′d < xq). Always check your equation gives back P = 0.5 at δ0.

Memory trick: "Current first, then E = V + jxI, then check P". Salient: xq gives the angle, Id corrects the emf.
